## 3. Use Case 2: Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs)

### (a) Before vs. after architecture

**Before (cloud/on-prem server-centric over Wi-Fi):** AMRs stream perception to a server and receive orders (HTTPS/WebRTC). Two documented failure modes: (1) **Makino** — Wi-Fi handover delays between access points destabilized AMR–server communication; robots stalled on roaming (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/makino-improves-performance-of-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-aws-wavelength-and-5g-network/). (2) A 600,000 sq-ft distribution center — Wi-Fi roaming dropped **400+ bots** moving at 30 mph mid-aisle; a disconnected bot halts; covering the space needed **~120 APs** (Celona, https://celona.io/resources/automated-distribution-center-bots-private-5g). Wi-Fi handover is client-side and takes **200 ms to a couple of seconds**; Wi-Fi 6 tail latencies during mobility reach **~264 ms** (https://www.aerix.uk/blog/wifi6-vs-private-5g-factory-decision; https://ijaidsml.org/index.php/ijaidsml/article/download/541/503).

**After (edge-distributed, two 2024 patterns):**
1. **On-device autonomy**: each robot carries an NPU (e.g., Cortex-A78 + 4 TOPS) running quantized ML, on-device SLAM, ROS 2 navigation, with peer-to-peer 802.11s mesh for fleet coordination — no cloud dependency for safety functions (Rapid Circuitry AMR platform, https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/edge-ai-warehouse-robotics).
2. **Edge-server offload over 5G**: compute moves to the network edge, not the robot. **Makino** moved control servers from factory premises to **AWS Wavelength** (AWS compute inside KDDI's 5G base stations, no internet traversal), deployed in **<5 months**, choosing public 5G + Wavelength over building private 5G for "significant cost savings" (AWS blog above; https://aws-news.com/article/2023-09-11-makino-improves-performance-of-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-aws-wavelength-and-5g-network). The **E5SH** agricultural robot showed edge-server-over-5G delivers **>18-fold peak processing speedup** vs. a standalone Jetson Xavier NX (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/rob.22384). Meanwhile **Celona private 5G (CBRS)** replaced ~120 Wi-Fi APs with **28** and onboard cellular gateways per bot.

### (b) Quantified impacts

| Metric | Wi-Fi/cloud-centric | Edge/5G result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Handover/roaming | 200 ms–2 s pauses; bots drop and halt | Network-controlled 5G handover in **tens of ms**; **~61,000 handovers/day, zero dropped bots** | Aerix; Celona |
| Tail latency | Wi-Fi 6 up to ~264 ms during mobility | Private 5G **<45 ms at 99.99th percentile** (5.9× better: 264/45) | ijaidsml study |
| Control-loop latency (lab) | — | 5G URLLC: **≤1 ms for 99.9%** of 100,000 OTA packets (outliers ~2 ms), on-prem 5G core | RWTH Aachen, https://publications.rwth-aachen.de/record/848246/files/848246.pdf |
| Access latency (carrier edge) | >100 ms via internet path | Wavelength: single-digit ms access; KDDI measured **RTT −40–50% vs 4G** | AWS; KDDI, https://news.kddi.com/kddi/corporate/english/newsrelease/2020/12/16/4980.html |
| Availability | Bots halt on roaming loss | **−90% downtime**; bot downtime ~$50k/day (industry estimate, not customer-reported) | Celona |
| Throughput/economics | Wi-Fi + fixed-line baseline | **+35% packages/yr (+180k), >$800k throughput value, >$1.1M downtime/labor/maintenance savings** in a 220k sq-ft warehouse | ABI Research/Globalstar, https://www.globalstar.com/getmedia/96e241ab-a868-45c3-922b-11e89d7d5fcb/abi-research-private-5g-in-warehouses.pdf |

An important 2024 nuance from Makino's own engineers: for AMR logistics, **"ultra-stability" beats ultra-low latency** — sub-10 ms is unnecessary (their illustration: a car at 50 km/h covers ~1.4 m in 100 ms, so braking control needs 1 ms-class latency, but a warehouse AMR does not); the decisive win was eliminating handover stalls (https://atmarkit.itmedia.co.jp/ait/articles/2107/27/news025.html).

### (c) Trade-offs

- **Cost.** Private 5G startup cost is **€500k–2M for a medium plant**, with talent scarcity the most underestimated barrier (https://jacar.es/en/private-5g-networks-in-factories-when-it-makes-sense/); Wi-Fi 6 remains cheaper for stationary, tolerance-friendly fleets. Offsets: 28 vs ~120 APs in the Celona case is a (120−28)/120 = **76.7% reduction (~4.3×)** — Celona's "up to 10×" is a general claim, not this deployment's; less cabling/maintenance; and P5G can cut TCO **up to 53%** in facilities >100k sq ft via avoided downtime (ijaidsml). IEEE's 2024 techno-economic analysis found 5G-based centralized AMR control beats a human-based process on TCO after **~2.5 years** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/MCOM.005.2400125). Makino shows the middle path: public 5G + Wavelength avoids private-network capex at the price of carrier dependency.
- **Security.** Private cellular offers SIM-based encryption and keeps sensitive control traffic on-premises — a stated reason mission-critical IIoT verticals choose it (ABI via https://www.technologyforyou.org/cost-security-and-throughput-the-iot-dilemma-when-choosing-a-cellular-or-non-cellular-private-wireless-network/). Counterweight: a centralized edge-control server is a single high-value target, and carrier-hosted Wavelength introduces trust in a third party's infrastructure.
- **Maintainability.** Fewer APs and network-controlled handover simplify RF engineering (Celona); Makino gained a "serverless AMR system" with remote monitoring, transferring server maintenance to AWS. On-device autonomy inverts this: no network dependency, but every robot needs OTA model management (the same blue/green problem as Use Case 1).

## 4. Use Case 3: Energy Distribution (Grid Edge)

### (a) Before vs. after architecture

**Before (centralized SCADA/DMS):** Field IEDs/RTUs → telemetry → centralized Distribution Management System; FLISR (fault location, isolation, service restoration) decided centrally. Documented weaknesses: "long fault processing time, due to centralized decision making" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/c8ykk94jzd9); existing communications are "centralized at the distribution management system, with very little autonomy or intelligence at the grid-edge" (OSTI HIL testbed, https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1885228). SA Power Networks could register only **80,000 data points**, and rural fault location was slow across a network with thin SCADA coverage (https://www.se.com/us/en/work/campaign/customer-stories/sa-power-networks/). Even modernized *centralized* self-healing (Brazil's ENERGISA MS, 293 reclosers) restored **3,093 consumers in 15 s and 316 in 40 s** (https://www.academia.edu/121720104/).

**After (edge-distributed, 2024 state of the art):** Three latency tiers:
1. **Protection (ms-class, substation edge):** UK Power Networks' **Constellation** project — the "world's first smart substation" — runs powerful computers in substations so operation is "decentralized," reducing "reliance on communications to and from the central control systems"; three vendors' applications (GE Vernova PhasorController, ABB, Siemens) run on one "Constellation Cubical" rack (https://www.gevernova.com/software/customer-stories/uk-power-networks-uses-ge-vernova-grid-software-worlds-first-smart-substation; https://www.analysysmason.com/contentassets/d9fba902675f49888498edaabe43c458/analysys_mason_renewable_energy_edge_driver_dec2023_rma08_rma04_rma18.pdf). ABB's **SSC600/SW** virtualized protection consolidates up to 30 bays per unit and runs on VMware Edge Compute Stack/Linux KVM on standard Xeon servers; an ABB–Caruna real-substation pilot showed real-time performance "comparable to existing non-virtualized solutions" (https://digitalsubstation.com/en/article/virtualized-protection-with-r-goose-over-5g-the-constellation-field-trial-by-ukpn; https://library.e.abb.com/public/a49d441fa1144b4da958617292170971/EL_GBL_2023_ELDS_DA_SSC600_Q4_white_paper.pdf). LF Energy **SEAPATH** (National Grid + GE Vernova) achieved **4–5 ms round-trip GOOSE protection latency** via CPU isolation, IRQ offloading, PCI passthrough (https://lfenergy.org/national-grid-electricity-transmission-and-ge-vernova-collaborate-on-lf-energy-seapath-to-advance-virtualized-protection-and-control/).
2. **FLISR/self-healing (sub-second, feeder edge):** Distributed FLISR with peer-to-peer smart terminal units on industrial Ethernet — no central master — achieved **service restoration within 1 s** in SGCC's Xiamen pilot (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/0ed7/67d0e922da62b7a0e509fbb3ca2caf7f86c7.pdf). Irish research (2024) moves subsets of grid topology and FLISR logic onto **low-cost edge devices on existing infrastructure**, fault-tolerant and "not fully reliant on a centralized cloud deployment" (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.17497). China's first 5G+MEC distribution-automation deployment pairs edge servers with local terminal units to shorten fault processing time (https://exa.ai/library/publication/c8ykk94jzd9).
3. **Cloud (digital twin, verification):** cloud-edge fault diagnosis keeps routine faults on an edge fast path and escalates hard DER/topology cases: **118 ms median decision latency, 98.4% section-level accuracy, 31.5 kB uplink per event** instead of continuous raw-waveform upload (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vf860xyfqmq).

### (b) Quantified impacts

| Metric | Centralized baseline | Edge-distributed result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protection latency | — | **4–5 ms RTT** (GOOSE, virtualized platform) | LF Energy SEAPATH |
| FLISR restoration | 15–40 s (centralized ADMS); minutes–hours manual | **<1 s** (distributed, Xiamen) → **15–40× faster** (1 s vs 15–40 s) | CIRED 2017; Academia.edu |
| Customers impacted / outage time | — | FLISR cuts customers impacted **up to 45%** and outage time **up to 51%** | OSTI (citing lit.) |
| Outage frequency | — | **~20% reduction in outages**, 10–15% lower network losses (Elektrodistribucija Srbije, 3.8M customers) | https://findausecase.com/use-cases/elektrodistribucija-srbije-modernizes-its-grid-with-schneider-electric-s-ecostruxure-adms-and-derms |
| Restoration at scale | — | **350,000 households restored in <20 s** (Tata Power self-healing grid) | https://download.se.com/files?p_Doc_Ref=998-20186520_GMA-US |
| Monitoring density | 80,000 data points | **1,000,000 data points (12.5×)** with faster FLISR (SA Power Networks) | Schneider |
| Uplink bandwidth | Continuous raw-waveform upload | **31.5 kB/event** (edge feature compression + topology-masked GNN) | exa.ai cloud-edge DA paper |
| Capacity unlocked | — | **+1.4 GW** network capacity, **>£750M** consumer savings and −17.8 Mt GHG by 2050 (UKPN Constellation) | GE Vernova |

### (c) Trade-offs

- **Cost.** Constellation is funded by Ofgem's Network Innovation Competition at **£17.82M (2021–2026)** — i.e., this architecture still needs subsidy-scale investment to prove out (digitalsubstation.com). Offsets: virtualized protection replaces panels of dedicated relays (one SSC600 unit ≤30 bays); Irish FLISR uses low-cost edge devices on *existing* grid infrastructure; SEAPATH is open-source, reducing licensing lock-in. Schneider's ADMS deployments (Austin Energy: FLISR + Volt-VAR live in <2 years) show commercial off-the-shelf paths (https://www.casestudies.com/company/schneider-electric/case-study/austin-energy-leverages-ecostruxure-for-utility-solution-to-improve-energy-efficiency).
- **Security.** The grid edge is the hardest security case: OSTI notes FLISR communications "must be resilient to natural disasters or cyberattacks," and pub-sub architectures like OpenFMB are proposed precisely to keep low-latency device-to-device exchange working when backhaul fails. More edge nodes = more NERC-CIP/IEC-62443-scoped assets; R-GOOSE over 5G (Constellation) requires rigorous key management. Virtualization adds a specific new risk class: GE Vernova's VPAC white paper stresses that **low latency and determinism are not inherent** in virtualized protection — hyperthreading introduced trip-time jitter, requiring VM pinning and CPU isolation (https://www.gevernova.com/electrification/sites/default/files/2026-08/GE%20Vernova-VPAC-Testing-White%20Paper-082026_opt.pdf).
- **Maintainability.** Positive: software-only protection enables remote deployment and faster upgrades, and hardware independence (ABB SSC600 SW) plus multi-vendor coexistence on one substation computer (UKPN). Negative: dependence on third-party industrial servers and hypervisors creates new failure/maintenance domains, and multi-vendor integration raises commissioning complexity.

# Telehealth Platform Design for Low-Connectivity Rural Primary Care in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania: Asynchronous Workflows, Offline-First Architecture, and Diagnostic UX

## 1. Scope and evidence base

This report synthesizes the available evidence on (a) how asynchronous communication, offline-first architecture, and diagnostic workflow design affect consultation quality and outcomes in low-connectivity settings; (b) a comparative UX analysis of Babyl (Babylon Health's Rwanda deployment), mPharma's telemedicine interface, and Zipline's tools; (c) the specific interaction patterns associated with consultation completion above 85% and diagnostic accuracy comparable to in-person care; and (d) cognitive load principles for clinical forms and image capture under low digital proficiency and frequent network interruptions.

The strongest quantitative evidence comes from: Babyl's administrative dataset of 3,899,788 consultations (2019–2023) analyzed via interrupted time series against Rwanda's HMIS (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12875-026-03179-8); a standardized-patient (SP) study of 1,459 in-person and 1,218 Babyl telemedicine visits (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf); a randomized crossover teleconsultation concordance trial in rural India (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10337309/); the IDinsight quasi-experimental evaluation of Zipline Ghana (https://www.idinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Zipline-Brief-FINAL-Digital-v3.pdf); the inSCALE cluster RCT in Uganda (https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article/file?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pdig.0000217&type=printable); and the WHO 2019 guideline on digital interventions (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541898/). Important caveats on evidence quality appear in Section 9.

---

## 2. Finding 1: Asynchronous communication patterns — effects on quality and outcomes

**Asynchrony itself does not degrade diagnostic accuracy.** In the rural India randomized crossover trial (104 patients, 10 clinics, blinded in-person vs. remote doctors), there was no significant association between diagnostic or treatment concordance and consultation mode (synchronous vs. asynchronous; P = .32 and P = .29 respectively), consultation order (P = .65, P = .81), or health-worker–doctor pairing (both P = .93). Overall concordance was 74% (77/104) diagnostic and 79.8% (83/104) treatment — within the 73–99% range reported globally for telemedicine vs. face-to-face concordance. Accuracy was driven by **case type**, not modality: hypertension 95% (20/21, Cohen's κ = 0.93) and diabetes 93% (14/15, κ = 0.89) versus 30% (3/10) for nonspecific symptoms and 33% (1/3) for cardiology (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10337309/). Design implication: asynchronous channels are safe for protocolized, symptom-definable conditions and unsafe as the sole pathway for undifferentiated presentations, which need explicit escalation to synchronous or in-person care.

**Structured store-and-forward works at very low bandwidth and low cost.** The Médecins Sans Frontières store-and-forward network processed >1,000 specialist cases from 40 countries over unreliable field connections, with stable process-quality and user-value scores over a 9-month monitoring period (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2014.00082/full). A pediatric endocrine SAF network (81 referrers, 88% in Haiti; 13 specialists; 47 cases; 412 messages, median 7 per case, IQR 5–11) achieved 100% "appropriate expert consulted and answer provided sufficiently quickly," 86% "answer well-adapted to my environment," 72% "able to follow the advice," 88% diagnosis clarification, and 93% management assistance (https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2019.00272/pdf). The median of ~7 structured messages per case is a useful sizing benchmark: SAF consultations are multi-turn but bounded.

**The bandwidth arithmetic strongly favors store-and-forward over live video on 2G.** Illustrative calculation using teledermatology image standards (minimum 800×600 px ≈ 0.8 MP, JPEG compression no greater than 20:1; https://gtp.health.mil/content/pdf/photoguide.pdf): 0.8 MP × 3 bytes/pixel ≈ 2.4 MB uncompressed → ~120 KB at 20:1 compression ≈ 960 kilobits. On a GPRS link (~40 kbps effective) that transfers in ~24 seconds; on EDGE (~100 kbps effective) in ~10 seconds. Live interactive video, by contrast, requires ≥384 kbps for 4CIF@30fps per the same standards — roughly 4–10× the realistic capacity of 2G links. A single still image plus structured history therefore delivers diagnostic-grade content in seconds on networks where live video is impossible.

**Low-bandwidth channels outperformed richer channels for outcomes.** In the WHO-commissioned meta-analysis of telemedicine for diabetes care in LMICs (31 interventions), telephone- and SMS-based interventions yielded the largest treatment effects compared with telemetry- and smartphone-app-based services (HbA1c SMD −0.38, 95% CI −0.52 to −0.23; adherence SMD 0.81, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.42) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7941107/). This is direct evidence that voice + SMS is not a degraded fallback but the highest-yield channel set for chronic disease follow-up in these settings.

**Asynchronous provider-to-provider teleconsultation sustains high response rates — with a load caveat.** The Addis Clinic's Kenya P2P platform (430 frontline health workers, 117 remote specialists) flagged 99% of 726 baseline cases as "answered," but only 75% of 3,548 cases during the pandemic-year surge (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2022.1028999/full). Completion above 85% is achievable asynchronously, but requires surge capacity planning; a 24-percentage-point drop under 5× volume is the observed failure mode.

---

## 3. Finding 2: Offline-first architecture — effects on quality and outcomes

**Architecture principles with documented field performance.** The Community Health Toolkit (CHT), deployed at national scale in Kenya (eCHIS) and Uganda, defines offline-first as "the application never relies on an internet connection for day to day tasks": all forms, contact data, and task lists are cached on-device; code updates are checked in the background and the user is *not* notified if the check fails or times out, so workflows continue uninterrupted; update prompts are dismissible so a user mid-form (e.g., "creating a contact or completing a form") never loses progress; sync happens opportunistically when connectivity returns, with explicit conflict-resolution machinery (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/). These are directly transferable interaction patterns: non-blocking background sync, dismissible update prompts, device-resident forms, and deferred upload.

**Outcome evidence that CHW-facing mHealth improves care.** The inSCALE cluster RCT in Uganda (39 sub-counties, 3,167 CHWs) found mHealth support increased appropriate treatment of malaria, diarrhoea, and pneumonia per national guidelines by 11% versus control (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.02–1.21; p = 0.018), with the largest point estimate for diarrhoea (RR 1.39, 95% CI 0.90–2.15) (https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article/file?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pdig.0000217&type=printable). This is the clearest experimental evidence that mobile tooling for low-proficiency users improves clinical quality at scale — and the mechanisms the authors credit (increased confidence, connectedness, supervision) are UX-mediated.

## 4. Finding 3: Diagnostic workflow design — the Rwanda evidence

The Babyl SP study is the most rigorous head-to-head comparison of telemedicine vs. in-person diagnostic workflow in East Africa (1,459 in-person visits to 81 facilities; 1,218 audio-only Babyl calls; standardized malaria, viral URI, and diarrhea cases; https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf):

- **Malaria (protocolized, test-dependent):** correct case management (ordering microscopy or RDT) was statistically indistinguishable between telemedicine and in-person care.
- **Viral URI (high-discretion, over-treatment-prone):** SPs were almost 30% more likely to receive correct case management (no unnecessary labs/antibiotics) via Babyl. Providers found it "easier to say no over the phone" — when SPs requested an unnecessary antibiotic, in-person providers capitulated more often. Telemedicine reduced bias in prescribing.
- **Efficiency:** telemedicine providers gathered *more* history in *shorter* consultations; patients waited ~1 hour less; out-of-pocket costs were lower; fewer labs were ordered in both cases.
- **Safety valve:** the diarrhea case tested whether remote providers correctly recognized and referred emergent cases requiring physical exam — the referral pathway is a designed, measured component of the workflow, not an afterthought.

The platform-level workflow that enabled this: patient dials *811# (USSD/voice, feature-phone compatible) → nurse or GP audio consultation → three possible loop-closing outcomes: (1) SMS prescription code redeemable at partner pharmacies, decoded by a Babyl agent; (2) SMS lab-test code executed at a partner lab, with results returned to Babyl and the provider contacting the patient to *continue the consultation* (a store-and-forward loop closure); (3) referral to a conventional facility when physical exam is needed (same source; also https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf).

Population-level outcomes (interrupted time series, n = 3,899,788 consultations; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12875-026-03179-8): Babyl's introduction produced immediate reductions in facility-based cases — respiratory infections −1,055 cases/month (95% CI −1,098 to −1,011; P < .001), malaria −246 (95% CI −258 to −234), gastritis −137 (95% CI −146 to −127), UTI −114 (95% CI −124 to −105). After Babyl's September 2023 shutdown, facility demand reversed (monthly increases of 1 case for gastritis/diarrhea/UTI to 10 for respiratory infections) — a natural-experiment demonstration that the telemedicine channel had genuinely absorbed and then released primary care demand.

**Babyl — voice-first asynchrony with human-agent loop closure.** The decisive UX choice was making the *patient-side* interface channel-agnostic (USSD/voice/SMS on any phone) and delegating all smartphone-dependent steps (code decoding, registration assistance) to a human agent network embedded in 450–501 health facilities (https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13041620/). The failure modes were also UX-relevant: medication stock-outs and inability to reach consultations eroded provider enthusiasm; lapsed users reported satisfaction but discontinued due to *process friction*; active users needed 2–3 attempts before routine use.

**mPharma — relocate the connectivity and the examination.** mPharma's "Telemedicine 2.0" insight is architectural: rather than pushing telemedicine into low-bandwidth homes, it anchors consultations at mutti pharmacies, where a licensed community health nurse operates a Tytocare all-in-one digital stethoscope, otoscope, thermometer, and examination camera ("high-definition skin and throat images") while the doctor consults remotely, with rapid diagnostic tests on site (https://techcrunch.com/2021/10/11/mpharma-a-telehealth-pioneer-out-of-ghana-gets-physical-with-100-virtual-centers-across-africa/; https://medium.com/mpharma-insights/telemedicine-2-0-mpharmas-vision-to-transform-primary-care-in-africa-576fad3152cb). **Zipline — channel redundancy and inventory truth as clinical decision support.** Zipline is a logistics platform, not a consultation platform; its "clinical decision tools" are the ordering and inventory interfaces. For your platform, Zipline's lesson is that medication reconciliation in rural settings is upstream of the UI: a consultation that ends in a prescription the pharmacy cannot fill destroys completion and trust — Babyl's stock-out-driven provider frustration and mPharma's vendor-managed inventory both confirm this.

## 6. Interaction patterns achieving >85% completion and in-person-comparable accuracy

**Completion above 85%:**

1. **Voice/USSD-first intake with no app install** (Babyl *811#): overall completion >94% across all appointment categories; 94.3% for respiratory consultations and 87% for malaria cases requiring lab confirmation — a 7.3 pp gap attributable to lab-dependency, both above the 85% threshold (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12875-026-03179-8). The same paper contrasts this with 15–30% dropout in Nigerian digital health pilots, attributing the difference to insurance integration and e-prescription loop closure.
2. **Nurse-led structured triage with physician escalation:** triage nurses managed 44.2% and senior nurses 25.6% of consultations (69.8% nurse-managed), exceeding India's eSanjeevani (~45%), with Rwanda's standardized triage protocols and real-time physician backup credited for provider confidence. Note triage-level appointments had the highest no-show rate (3.6% vs. 1.0% GPs, 1.1% senior nurses) — the entry tier is the leakiest and needs the most friction removal.
3. **Closed-loop SMS codes with a human agent at the redemption point:** the prescription/lab code → agent-decoded → results-returned → consultation-resumed cycle keeps every state transition confirmable without data connectivity.
4. **Bounded multi-turn asynchronous case packages** (median 7 messages/case) with in-country triage coordinators: 99% answered at baseline load (Addis Clinic), 100% timely expert response (pediatric endocrine network).
5. **Channel-redundant ordering** (text/mobile/web) so the interaction never blocks on a single network state (Zipline).

**Diagnostic accuracy comparable to in-person:**

1. **Protocolized condition routing:** the SP study found malaria case-management parity with in-person care and ~30% *better* URI management (less over-treatment) via audio-only telemedicine (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).
2. **Mode-independence of accuracy:** synchronous vs. asynchronous mode showed no significant concordance difference (P = .32/.29), so store-and-forward can be the default with synchronous reserved for escalation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10337309/).
3. **Embedded digital assistants:** use of a digital assistant to facilitate consultations "resulted in increased adherence to evidence-based care protocols" in the India trial — structured, guided data entry outperformed free-form history.
4. **Clinician-operated image capture:** SAF teledermatology outcomes with clinician-submitted images were comparable to in-person visits, while patient-submitted images showed lower and more variable quality and concordance (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302578/) — capture quality, not transmission technology, is the accuracy bottleneck.
5. **Explicit referral safety valves for undifferentiated presentations**, where concordance collapses to 30–33% without them (India trial; Babyl's diarrhea-referral case design).

## 7. Cognitive load principles for clinical forms and image capture

**Why it matters here.** Cognitive load theory holds that working memory is finite; when interfaces exceed it, information is lost and care quality degrades, and overloaded providers are hypothesized to deliver poorer, more stereotype-influenced care (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6703991/). **Evidence-based design levers:**

2. **Minimize mental operators, not just taps.** A GOMS cognitive task analysis of a mobile personal health record found 398 steps across 10 tasks, with mental operators consuming 73–76% of total task completion time; the authors' core recommendation is to reduce the number of mental operators (recall, decision, search) rather than physical actions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10651402/). Practically: one decision per screen, pre-populated defaults from prior encounters, visible progress, and no requirement to remember data from earlier screens.
3. **Design for interruption as the normal case.** WHO documents (high confidence) that rural workers face poor connectivity and power, and (low confidence) that SMS character limits, small screens, broken local-language fonts, and note-taking hostility degrade usability (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541898/). # Research Report: The "Bubble Gum" 5K at California's Great America

**No 5K race with the literal words "bubble gum" in its title could be verified as having been hosted at the Great America theme park in Santa Clara, California.** The race that matches this description — and the one that search activity clearly associates with "bubble gum" + Great America queries — is the **Bubble Run 5K**, a bubble/foam-themed fun run held at California's Great America. The most likely explanation is that the event's title is "Bubble Run" (bubble, not bubble gum), and it is frequently misremembered as a "Bubble Gum Run."

## Supporting Evidence

**1. The Bubble Run 5K at California's Great America**
- Facebook's answer page for the query "Bubble Gum Great America Run" states directly: "The Bubble Run event at California's Great America features a fun 5K run through colorful foam and bubbles... Registration normally costs $54.95... The event is family-friendly and suitable for all ages... untimed and non-competitive" (https://www.facebook.com/fb-answers/bubble-gum-great-america-run/).
- The event organizer's official site confirms the format: "A family-friendly, non-competitive 5K through mountains of colorful bubbles... wear white, leave covered in foam," running since 2012 with 500+ events across the US (https://bubblerun.com/).
- Instagram topic pages auto-generated from the exact search phrase "bubble gum 5k great america california" surface Bubble Run content tagged alongside the park's official @cagreatamerica account — e.g., "Not your average 5k race... Bubble Run participants run, walk, dance and play across 3 miles of bubbly fun!" (https://www.instagram.com/popular/bubble-gum-5k-great-america-california/ and https://www.instagram.com/popular/5k-race-great-america-theme-park-california-bubble-gum/). This indicates the public query "bubble gum 5k Great America" resolves to the Bubble Run event.

**2. A phonetic near-match: the "Run Forrest Run 5K" presented by Bubba Gump Shrimp Co.**
If the question stems from a "bubble gum"-*sounding* name, the other 5K hosted at the park was the **Run Forrest Run 5K**, presented by the **Bubba Gump Shrimp Company** (phonetically close to "bubble gum"). Details from listings:
- "Bubba Gump Shrimp Company presents the seventh annual 5K fun run and walk inside the amusement park. Proceeds benefit the United Way of Silicon Valley. Free parking and admission to Great America after the race" — held Sunday, September 14, 2008, 7:55 a.m., cost $20–$30, at California's Great America, 2401 Agnew Rd, Santa Clara (https://www.sanjose.com/run-forrest-run-5k-e330431).
- A participant account of the 2009 edition (September 20, 2009, 8:05 a.m. start) notes "1000+ Runners and Walkers at Great America for this 7th annual truly unique 5K Fun Run and Walk inside of No. California's most thrilling Family Park" (http://motastic145.blogspot.com/2009/10/fff-diva-activity-running-5k-bubba-gump.html; also https://unilocal.net/united-states/santa-clara/bubba-gump-shrimp-cos-run-forrest-run-5k-fun-run).

Genuine "bubble gum"-titled races exist, but none at Great America:

## Context on the Venue

The "old Great America theme park in California" is California's Great America in Santa Clara, which opened March 20, 1976 as Marriott's Great America, later operated as Paramount's Great America and then under Cedar Fair/Six Flags, and is expected to close after the 2027 season absent a lease extension (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California's_Great_America).

The best-supported answer is the **Bubble Run 5K** at California's Great America — the bubble-themed 5K that people searching "bubble gum 5k Great America" are actually recalling — with the **Run Forrest Run 5K (Bubba Gump Shrimp Co.)** as the phonetic alternative. # Multimodal Checkout for Blind and Low-Vision Shoppers: Evidence Synthesis on Voice-Only vs. Hybrid Touch-with-Audio Workflows

## 1. Scope and an honest note on the evidence base

No published study was found that directly randomizes blind/low-vision (BLV) participants between "sequential voice-only checkout" and "hybrid touch-with-audio-feedback checkout" for a 15+ item grocery cart. The evidence below is therefore triangulated from four adjacent literatures: (a) assistive-technology input studies with BLV participants (eyes-free numeric entry, gesture calculators, screen-reader shopping), (b) general modality-comparison experiments (voice vs. touch vs. multimodal) with workload measurement, (c) mobile commerce usability and accessibility auditing, and (d) WCAG 2.2 guidance and implementation case studies. Where a figure comes from a sighted or older-adult population, or from a non-shopping task, that limitation is stated explicitly. All arithmetic is shown inline.

---

## 2. Task completion rates

**Baseline gap between BLV screen-reader users and sighted users is large.** In the Nielsen Norman Group program of usability tests (104 total participants; quantitative arm: 20 screen-reader users, 20 screen-magnifier users, 20 sighted controls, four tasks including an e-commerce purchase), success rates averaged **12.5% for screen-reader users, 21.4% for magnifier users, and 78.2% for controls** — controls completed tasks at **6.3× the rate of screen-reader users** (78.2 / 12.5 = 6.26), with time-on-task of 16:46 vs. 7:14 and 2.0 vs. 0.6 errors (https://media.nngroup.com/media/reports/free/Usability_Guidelines_for_Accessible_Web_Design.pdf). Note this is 2001 desktop data; treat magnitude as directional, not current.

**Abandonment is the dominant failure mode in commerce specifically.** Nucleus Research's interview study with 73 blind adults found **more than 70% of sites inaccessible, blind users abandoning ~two transactions per month, and roughly two-thirds of transactions ending in abandonment** (https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/153358/Nucleus-The%20Internet%20is%20unavailable.pdf). Industry-side audits converge: average cart abandonment across 49 studies is 70.19%, and **89% of the top 100 US e-commerce sites have accessibility issues in checkout flows** (https://accessibe.com/blog/cart-abandonment-impact-for-ecommerce). The 2025 Ecommerce Accessibility Readiness Snapshot (250 pages manually audited against 15 WCAG 2.2 criteria across five European markets and five global marketplaces) scored **Cart 4.3/10, Delivery 4.4/10, Payment 5.1/10**, with **84% of audited pages failing to label checkout content for assistive technology** — i.e., checkout is frequently "invisible" to screen readers (https://join.contentsquare-foundation.org/hubfs/RM/2025/Ecomm%203%20pager%20English.pdf?hsLang=en; corroborated in the CHI 2026 scoping review, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772363.3799042). A usability-testing study estimating WCAG 2.1's protective power found it prevents only **41–71% of real accessibility problems**, with blind users overrepresented among unresolved issues (https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1784326/FULLTEXT01.pdf) — conformance alone will not guarantee completion.

**Voice-only shopping is feasible but fragile.** A CHI 2026 Wizard-of-Oz study of a voice-based computer-using agent with 12 visually impaired participants demonstrated end-to-end voice shopping from exploration to purchase decision, but participants needed compensatory strategies throughout (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791681). Earlier assistive shopping systems (RoboCart, ShopTalk/ShopMobile) achieved successful product acquisition with blind participants, but with speech interfaces imposing **higher frustration than typing interfaces** in NASA-TLX, and browsing-style interfaces slowest of all (5 blind + 5 sighted-blindfolded participants, 11,147-product database; https://www-robotics.usc.edu/~tapus/IROS2007/IROS2007Slides/iros07-Workshop-Gharpure.pdf).

---

## 3. Input error frequencies — especially numerical entry

This is the strongest-evidenced area, and it consistently favors **touch-plus-audio-feedback over both unassisted screen-reader targeting and unverified voice**.

**Screen-reader numeric targeting is slow and error-prone.** Baseline VoiceOver-style entry of four-digit PINs took **7.5 seconds (~0.53 characters/second)** with an uncorrected error rate of **6.43% (SD 7.16)**, versus **3.52% (SD 5.87)** for the Perkinput chorded method — VoiceOver's error rate was **1.83× higher** (6.43 / 3.52), a significant difference (F₁,₁₈₈₂ = 91.87, p < .0001) (University of Washington dissertation chapter covering DigiTaps/Perkinput, https://digital.lib.washington.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/b7fba4e3-b8eb-436e-9f81-54c8787e89ae/content).

**Audio feedback after every input buys accuracy at a speed cost.** DigiTaps (longitudinal study, 16 people incl. 6 blind): eyes-free number entry with **no audio feedback ran at 0.87 characters/second with a 5.63% uncorrected error rate (SD 14.8)**; adding audio feedback after every input made entry **slower but significantly more accurate** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2501988.2502056). Haptic-only feedback was faster but less accurate than audio. Design implication for quantity adjustment: per-entry spoken echo is the accuracy-preserving default; 0.87 vs. ~0.53 CPS means gesture-based entry is still ~64% faster (0.87 / 0.53 = 1.64) than screen-reader keypad targeting even *with* audio echo.

**Structured numeric gestures reduce erroneous outcomes, not just entry errors.** GestureCalc (8 screen-reader users, longitudinal): **40.5% faster entry and 52.2% fewer erroneous calculations** than a standard screen-reader calculator; participants made more raw mistakes but corrected more of them. Critically, the authors note that **error recovery in long calculations is costly because users must restart the expression from the beginning**, motivating a "readback" feature (shake to hear the entered expression) for long operands (https://faculty.washington.edu/wobbrock/pubs/assets-19.01.pdf; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3308561.3353783). In their pilot, expression-entry error was ≤3% and code-recall errors fell to 0 by session 2, with entry speed +24% from session 1 to 2 — learnability is real but requires repetition.

**Counter-style input beats keypad-style input for quantities.** A within-subject pilot (N=8 visually impaired + N=11 blindfolded-sighted controls) comparing multiple-choice, numeric keypad, tap-based counter, and shake-based counter found modality significantly affected completion time (p < .001), **mental demand (p = .045), effort (p = .039), and frustration (p = .011)**, with **counter-based modalities consistently more efficient and lower in cognitive load**, and navigation-dependent (keypad) input imposing measurable overhead (https://exa.ai/library/publication/t52dqv29zmc). For grocery quantity adjustment ("2 → 3 → 4" of apples), a stepper with per-step audio echo is better supported than free numeric entry.

**Voice entry: fast, fewer slips, but worse error *detection* — the dangerous combination for payments.** In sighted-population benchmarks (limitation noted), speech was **2.93–3.0× faster than touchscreen typing (153 vs. 52 WPM English)** with a corrected error rate of 5.30% vs. 11.22% (speech **52.8% lower**: (11.22 − 5.30) / 11.22 = 0.528) — but speech **left more errors in the final text (1.30% vs. 0.79% uncorrected, i.e., 64.6% higher**: (1.30 − 0.79) / 0.79 = 0.646) (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3161187; https://hci.stanford.edu/research/speech/paper/speech_paper.pdf). Real-time feedback during dictation cut user correction effort (10% vs. 14%, p = .04; https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~anujk1/CHI2012a_presentation.pdf). The decisive BLV-specific finding: when reviewing dictated text **by audio alone, blind participants identified only 40% of ASR errors** — statistically no better than sighted listeners' ~50% (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3382039). **Majority-of-errors-undetected** is the core risk of voice-only payment confirmation: a misheard "12" vs. "2" will most often survive audio review. A voice-billing design study similarly measured **47% recognition accuracy for conversational commands vs. 55% for short set-commands** — constrained command grammars outperform free conversation (https://www.dsource.in/sites/default/files/case-study/voice-assisted-billing-interface-vabi/introduction/file/Voice-Assisted-Billing-Interface-VABI.pdf).

**Security-sensitive numeric entry is a special case.** For PINs, auditory feedback is often prohibited; an NCR study of four touchscreen PIN concepts with visually impaired users found the **tactile-anchored concept best** (fixed tactile reference point for orientation) (https://publications.ergonomics.org.uk/uploads/Evaluating-touchscreen-PIN-entry-with-visually-impaired-users.pdf). BLV retail-checkout research echoes the privacy/risk anxiety around audible payment details and visible PIN entry (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3816243).

---

## 4. User confidence scores

- **NNGroup subjective rating (1–7, satisfaction/confidence/frustration composite):** screen-reader users **2.5**, magnifier users 2.9, controls 4.6; success score and subjective rating correlated at **r = 0.95** — confidence tracks completion almost perfectly, so anything that raises completion raises confidence (https://media.nngroup.com/media/reports/free/Usability_Guidelines_for_Accessible_Web_Design.pdf).
- **PSSUQ (7-point, higher = better) by input modality:** voice **4.70**, touch **5.21**, multimodal **5.47**; voice significantly lower on effectiveness, efficiency, comfort, and "liked using" subscales (all p ≤ .039) (Human Factors 2018 supplement, https://sage.cnpereading.com/storage/sage/journal/article/HFS/2018/HFS_2018_60_8/unzip/ds-hfs-10.1177_0018720818788995/Supplement_B_-_Results_for_Subjective_Measures_productionready(afterproofs).pdf). Caveat: this was an 18-participant sighted-population study (multi-UAV operation context), used here as general modality evidence, not BLV-specific data.
- **BLV self-efficacy in checkout contexts:** among 86 BLV survey respondents plus 10 contextual inquiries about retail self-checkout, **79% found in-store technology difficult or somewhat difficult, 65% rated it inaccessible, and current systems "negatively affected independence, self-efficacy, and equality"**; participants feared being charged incorrectly without knowing it (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3816243).
- **Learnability confidence:** GestureCalc participants "reported confidence in their ability to become fluent in practice" after session 2, despite acknowledging learning cost (https://faculty.washington.edu/wobbrock/pubs/assets-19.01.pdf). The CHI 2026 scoping review frames the design target as **"decision confidence"** — judging product suitability and transaction risk well enough to complete purchase without sighted help (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772363.3799042).

---

## 5. Voice-only vs. hybrid touch-with-audio: what the comparisons show

**Product selection.** Hybrid wins on preference and effectiveness. The EasyGO grocery field study found participants **preferred combined screen + audio cues over either alone, with audio-only second-best** — proactive audio was efficient but the screen preserved control (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656156.3663719). For physical reaching, speech+haptic multimodal feedback was the most effective and preferred mode (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3132525.3134817). For on-screen browsing, Slide Rule's audio-anchored multi-touch was faster than a button-based screen reader and preferred by 7/10 blind users, though with more errors (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1414471.1414487) — the recurring pattern: **hybrid touch+audio is faster and preferred; the error cost is managed by audio confirmation, not by abandoning touch.**

**Quantity adjustment.** See §3: tap-counter with per-step audio echo (DigiTaps/GestureCalc pattern) or stepper controls outperform both free voice ("add three") and screen-reader keypad entry. Voice quantity commands are acceptable for *initial* add-to-cart but should be echoed back and editable via touch.

**Payment confirmation.** Voice-only confirmation is the weakest link because (a) audio review catches <50% of speech errors (§3), (b) security constraints often forbid auditory feedback for PINs (§3), and (c) BLV users report elevated perceived financial risk when systems don't announce state (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3816243). Hybrid patterns — touch-anchored review with spoken read-back, or explicit voice confirmation *plus* a persistent, navigable review screen — align with both the AT literature and WCAG 3.3.4 (§6).

**General modality workload data (sighted N=18, non-shopping task — directional only).** Global NASA-RTLX: **voice 49.73 vs. touch 37.16 vs. multimodal 37.75** (voice +33.8% vs. touch: (49.73 − 37.16)/37.16 = 0.338; voice vs. touch p < .001, voice vs. multimodal p = .001). Mental demand 65.35 vs. 51.46/50.90 (+27.0%); temporal demand 69.31 vs. 44.10 (+57.2%); frustration 46.67 vs. 22.78 (**2.05×**); own-performance 64.65 vs. 82.50 (−21.6%); only physical demand favored voice (14.65 vs. 31.88). Situation awareness (3D-SART composite) dropped ~20.4% under voice (85.35 vs. 107.22). Preference rankings placed voice last; multimodal ≈ touch (https://sage.cnpereading.com/storage/sage/journal/article/HFS/2018/HFS_2018_60_8/unzip/ds-hfs-10.1177_0018720818788995/Supplement_B_-_Results_for_Subjective_Measures_productionready(afterproofs).pdf). A 40-day home deployment with older adults (Echo Dot voice-only vs. Echo Show voice+touch) found the touchscreen version cut setup time ~50% and latency ~20%, with touch used for ~27% of interactions — hybrid users selectively deploy touch to confirm (https://a11ybob.com/writing/reviews/69b2059145da129a951bec3b). Conversely, adding voice commands to an eyes-free browsing interface halved device-fixation time with unchanged cognitive-effort ratings (https://scholarworks.indianapolis.iu.edu/bitstreams/e42a592a-a060-4c67-a782-b442c4781f66/download) — voice's genuine advantage is hands/eyes-freeing, not workload reduction.

---

## 6. Cognitive load with 15+ item cart verification

No study measured workload specifically for verifying a 15+ item cart in a BLV checkout; the following converges on the answer:

1. **Voice is ephemeral; working memory saturates with list length.** In the CHI 2026 voice-CUA study, to "manage the cognitive load that arises from the ephemeral nature of voice interactions, users preferred concise summaries, a limited number of options, double-checking, and proactive guidance" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791681). A co-design study independently concluded a commerce VUI must provide "explicit confirmations and retrospective information from past shopping trips" because "failed speech recognition and overwhelming information had a negative impact" (https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1482523/FULLTEXT01.pdf).
2. **Workload scales with task load under every modality, but voice starts higher and degrades self-assessment.** In the NASA-RTLX experiment, high-load trials raised global workload from 37.42 to 45.68 (**+22.1%**: (45.68 − 37.42)/37.42) across all modalities, and the modality × task-load interaction on perceived own-performance was **stronger at high load** — i.e., voice's confidence penalty grows exactly when the verification burden grows (same supplement URL as §5).
3. **Audio-only verification of long sequences misses errors.** With 40% ASR-error detection by ear (§3) and GestureCalc's observation that long-expression recovery forces a full restart (§3), a 15-item spoken read-back is both high-load and low-yield. The voice-billing field study reported that manual long bills (7–8+ items) were "verified twice to prevent any calculation errors" — verification cost compounds with item count (https://www.dsource.in/sites/default/files/case-study/voice-assisted-billing-interface-vabi/introduction/file/Voice-Assisted-Billing-Interface-VABI.pdf).
4. **The audio channel is a scarce resource for BLV users.** For white-cane users, auditory guidance produced **22× higher cognitive load than haptic** feedback in short-range navigation (blindfolded controls showed no such gap — a warning against blindfolded-sighted-only testing) (https://www.lanfanshu.com/paper/61e5083616ad6f084cf62e43). A checkout that floods the audio channel with a 15-item read-back competes with the user's primary orientation channel.
5. **WCAG's own rationale confirms the memory mechanism:** Redundant Entry (3.3.7) exists because "requiring people to recall information previously entered can cause them to give up or re-enter the same information incorrectly," and its intent is to "reduce cognitive effort" in multi-step processes (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/redundant-entry.html).

**Net answer:** for 15+ item verification, voice-only sequential review imposes the highest cognitive load (highest mental/temporal demand, lowest situation awareness, worst self-rated performance, majority of errors undetected by ear). A hybrid pattern — persistent, screen-reader-navigable cart list with per-item jump-to-edit, chunked spoken summaries ("15 items, 4 produce, total €62.40; say 'review produce' or swipe to the list"), and item-level rather than whole-cart re-verification — is the evidence-aligned design.

---

## 7. What WCAG 2.2 case studies and guidance say about confirmation and error recovery

**Confirmation strategies (SC 3.3.4, Error Prevention — Legal, Financial, Data, Level AA).** For any financial transaction, at least one of: **Reversible** (submissions reversible), **Checked** (input errors checked with correction opportunity), or **Confirmed** (mechanism for reviewing, confirming, and correcting before finalizing). Sufficient techniques: **G98** (review and correct before submitting), **G155** (checkbox in addition to submit), **G164** (stated time within which the order may be amended/canceled), G99/G168 for deletions; advisory: SCR18 (client-side validation with alert) and G199 (success feedback on submission). The W3C's own example is an order-confirmation screen showing items, quantities, address, and payment method before final submit (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-prevention-legal-financial-data.html). WCAG2ICT extends these to non-web software, i.e., your mobile app (https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag2ict-22/).

**Redundant entry (SC 3.3.7, Level A).** Never ask for the same information twice in one process; auto-populate or make it selectable ("billing same as shipping" checkbox). Exceptions: essential re-entry, security, or invalidated data. Browser autocomplete is explicitly *not* sufficient (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/redundant-entry.html; implementation patterns: https://www.allaccessible.org/blog/wcag-337-redundant-entry-implementation-guide; https://traideas.github.io/wcag-training-suit/demos/3.3.7-redundant-entry/index.html).

**Accessible authentication (SC 3.3.8).** Permit pasting passwords/codes and support alternative authentication — no cognitive puzzles at login or payment (https://declareaccess.com/accessible-checkout-forms-ecommerce).

**Error recovery mechanics from implementation case studies.** Errors must be identified in text, tied to the field, and **announced via live regions (`role="alert"`/`aria-live`) — "otherwise a blind user never learns" an error occurred**; link label + invalid state + repair instruction through `aria-describedby` so the screen reader announces all three together on focus return; keep an optional "error fields only" view that preserves valid data and retains access to earlier details; test loading, out-of-stock, price-change, and declined-payment states, which is "where otherwise usable interfaces break down" (https://ecomdesignpro.com/ecommerce-form-errors/; https://declareaccess.com/accessible-checkout-forms-ecommerce; https://aedigitalagency.com/en/blog/ecommerce-accessibility-wcag-2-2-checkout; https://statutus.ch/en/guides/wcag-2-2-checklist-online-stores/). # Independent Directors Under the NASDAQ Listing Standards

## 1. Governing Rule and Core Definition

The NASDAQ independence requirements are set out in Listing Rule 5605 (Rule 5600 Series, Corporate Governance Requirements). Rule 5605(a)(2) defines an "Independent Director" as:

> "a person other than an Executive Officer or employee of the Company or any other individual having a relationship which, in the opinion of the Company's board of directors, would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment in carrying out the responsibilities of a director."

(Official rule text: https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series; see also the SEC-filed rule text at https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2013/34-68640-ex5.pdf and https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf.)

Two defined terms drive the definition:

- **"Executive Officer"** — those officers covered in Exchange Act Rule 16a-1(f) (i.e., the company's president, principal financial officer, principal accounting officer, vice presidents in charge of principal business functions, and policy-making officers) (Rule 5605(a)(1)).
- **"Family Member"** — "a person's spouse, parents, children, siblings, mothers and fathers-in-law, sons and daughters-in-law, brothers and sisters-in-law, and anyone (other than domestic employees) who shares such person's home." This definition was broadened in 2019–2020 (SR-NASDAQ-2019-049) to add parents-in-law and siblings-/sons-/daughters-in-law and to exclude non-resident stepchildren and domestic employees; the prior definition covered only "spouse, parents, children and siblings, whether by blood, marriage or adoption, or anyone residing in such person's home" (see https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/assets/rulebook/nasdaq/filings/SR-NASDAQ-2019-049_Notice.pdf and https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/02/20/2020-03320/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-notice-of-filing-of-amendment-no-3-and).

Interpretive material (IM-5605) adds that the reference to the "Company" in the rule includes any parent or subsidiary of the company, but is not intended to cover an entity whose ownership is reflected in the financial statements solely as an investment (https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series; https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2013/34-71037.pdf).

## 2. Eligibility Criteria (Who Qualifies)

NASDAQ's test is essentially a negative one — there are no affirmative qualifications (no minimum stock ownership, tenure, or credential requirements). A director qualifies as independent if:

1. **Not an insider**: The person is not an Executive Officer or employee of the Company (or its parents/subsidiaries).
2. **No judgment-impairing relationship**: The board, exercising its own opinion, concludes that no relationship the person has would interfere with independent judgment. The board must make an **affirmative determination** of independence — IM-5605 states the board "has a responsibility to make an affirmative determination that no such relationships exist through the application of Rule 5605(a)(2)" (https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).
3. **Fails no bright-line test**: The person does not fall within any of the categorical disqualifications in Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)–(F) (or, for investment companies, is not an "interested person" under paragraph (G)) — detailed in Section 3 below.
4. **Stock ownership alone is not disqualifying**: Nasdaq expressly does not believe that ownership of Company stock by itself precludes a finding of independence, so significant shareholders may serve as independent directors (IM-5605; https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

Domestic companies must disclose their independence determinations under Item 407(a) of Regulation S-K; Foreign Private Issuers must disclose in their next annual report (Form 20-F or 40-F) which directors the board has determined to be independent (Rule 5605(b)(1)).

## 3. Disqualification Criteria (Who Cannot Serve) — The Bright-Line Tests

Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)–(G) categorically precludes a finding of independence for:

**(A) Recent employment** — A director who is, or at any time during the past three years was, employed by the Company.

**(B) Excessive compensation** — A director who accepted, or has a Family Member who accepted, any compensation from the Company in excess of **$120,000** during any period of twelve consecutive months within the three years preceding the independence determination — **except**:
- (i) compensation for board or board committee service;
- (ii) compensation paid to a Family Member who is an employee (other than an Executive Officer) of the Company; and
- (iii) benefits under a tax-qualified retirement plan, or non-discretionary compensation.

Audit committee members are subject to additional, more stringent requirements under Rule 5605(c)(2).

**(C) Family ties to executive officers** — A director who is a Family Member of an individual who is, or at any time during the past three years was, employed by the Company as an Executive Officer.

**(D) Significant business transactions** — A director who is, or has a Family Member who is, a partner in, or a controlling Shareholder or an Executive Officer of, any organization to which the Company made, or from which the Company received, payments for property or services in the current or any of the past three fiscal years that exceed the **greater of 5% of the recipient's consolidated gross revenues for that year or $200,000** — **except** (i) payments arising solely from investments in the Company's securities, and (ii) payments under non-discretionary charitable contribution matching programs. IM-5605 confirms that under paragraph (D), a director (or one with a Family Member) who is an Executive Officer of a charitable organization is not independent if the Company's payments to that charity exceed the greater of 5% of the charity's revenues or $200,000 (https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series).

**(E) Interlocking compensation committees** — A director who is, or has a Family Member who is, employed as an Executive Officer of another entity where, at any time during the past three years, any of the Company's Executive Officers serve on that other entity's compensation committee.

**(F) Auditor relationships** — A director who is, or has a Family Member who is, a current partner of the Company's outside auditor, or who was a partner or employee of the outside auditor who worked on the Company's audit at any time during the past three years.

**(G) Investment companies** — In lieu of paragraphs (A)–(F), a director of an investment company who is an "interested person" of the Company as defined in Section 2(a)(19) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 — other than in his or her capacity as a board or board committee member — is not independent (harmonizing with the 1940 Act) (https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2013/34-68640-ex5.pdf).

**Mechanics of the look-back periods:** Per IM-5605, the three-year look-backs in paragraphs (A), (C), (E) and (F) commence on the date the relationship ceases — e.g., a director employed by the Company is not independent until three years after the employment terminates. Under paragraph (D), the measurement window is the current plus the past three fiscal years. Nasdaq staff interpretations also recognize narrow carve-outs reflected in company proxy disclosures — e.g., interim employment of less than one year that has since terminated does not disqualify under (A) or (B) (see, e.g., https://materials.proxyvote.com/Approved/053604/20220304/NPS_495509/26.html — a secondary source summarizing Nasdaq staff guidance).

**Additional stringency for committee service:** Beyond 5605(a)(2), audit committee members must also satisfy SEC Rule 10A-3(b)(1) independence (no consulting/advisory/compensatory fees other than board service; not an affiliated person of the Company), must not have participated in preparing the Company's financial statements in the past three years, and must be financially literate, with at least one member having financial sophistication (Rule 5605(c)(2)). Compensation committee members must be Independent Directors, and the board must additionally consider the source of the director's compensation and any affiliation that would impair judgment (Rule 5605(d)(2); https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2013/34-71037.pdf). Under "exceptional and limited circumstances," one non-independent director (who is not a current Executive Officer, employee, or Family Member of an Executive Officer) may serve on the audit or compensation committee for up to two years with disclosure; such a director may not chair the audit committee (Rule 5605(c)(2)(B), (d)(2)(B)).

## 4. Which Companies Must Have Independent Directors

**Baseline requirement — all operating companies with listed voting equity.** Rule 5605(b)(1) requires that "a majority of the board of directors must be comprised of Independent Directors as defined in Rule 5605(a)(2)." Quantitatively, for a board of N directors, independent directors must number at least ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 — e.g., a 7-member board needs at least 4 independent directors; an 8-member board needs at least 5. Rule 5605(b)(2) also requires regularly scheduled executive sessions of independent directors (at least twice a year is contemplated, per IM-5605-2). The Federal Register confirms that Nasdaq rules require "a majority of the board... be Independent Directors, and that the company's audit, compensation and nominating committees be comprised solely of Independent Directors" (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/09/19/2019-20220/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-order-instituting-proceedings-to-determine).

**Committee requirements** (for companies subject to Rule 5605):
- **Audit committee** (Rule 5605(c)(2)): at least 3 members, each an Independent Director under 5605(a)(2) plus Rule 10A-3(b)(1) independence.
- **Compensation committee** (Rule 5605(d)(2)): at least 2 members, each an Independent Director (plus the fee-source and affiliation considerations noted above).
- **Nominations committee** (Rule 5605(e)): comprised entirely of Independent Directors — or the company may forgo a committee and rely on a majority of the Independent Directors to discharge nomination responsibilities.

**Exemptions — companies not (fully) required to have independent directors:**

1. **Controlled Companies** (Rule 5615(a)(7)): a Company of which **more than 50% of the voting power for the election of directors** is held by an individual, a group, or another company is exempt from the majority-independent-board (5605(b)), compensation committee (5605(d)), and nominations (5605(e)) requirements — but not from the executive-session requirement (5605(b)(2)) or the audit committee requirements. Reliance must be disclosed (https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf).
2. **Foreign Private Issuers** (Rule 5615(a)(3)): may follow home country practice in lieu of the Rule 5600 Series (including the independent-director requirements), provided they comply with the Notification of Noncompliance (Rule 5625) and Voting Rights (Rule 5640) requirements, have an audit committee satisfying Rule 5605(c)(3) whose members meet the Rule 5605(c)(2)(A)(ii) independence criteria, and disclose each requirement not followed and the home country practice substituted (https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series; https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/assets/rulebook/nasdaq/filings/SR-NASDAQ-2024-019_Resubmission.pdf).
3. **Issuers of only non-voting preferred, debt, or derivative securities** (Rule 5615(a)(6)): exempt from the independent director, compensation committee, nominations, code of conduct, and shareholder meeting requirements; audit committee requirements apply only to the extent of SEC Rule 10A-3 (https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2025/34-102513-ex5.pdf).
4. **Asset-backed issuers and passive issuers** (e.g., unit investment trusts without a board) (IM-5615-1): Rules 5605(b), (c), (d), (e) and 5610 do not apply (https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/Nasdaq%205600%20Series).

**Phase-in schedules (Rule 5615(b))** — new or transitioning companies get time to comply:
- **IPO companies**: 12 months from the Listing Date to meet the majority-independent-board requirement; audit committee phases in (1 independent member by listing, majority within 90 days, all within one year); compensation and nominations committees phase in on the same schedule (https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf).
- **Companies emerging from bankruptcy, transferring from other exchanges or from Section 12(g) registration, or listing via carve-out/spin-off**: similar 12-month phase-ins (with audit committee composition generally required at listing, subject to committee-size phase-in for 12(g) companies) (same source; https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/assets/rulebook/NASDAQ/filings/SR-NASDAQ-2023-023.pdf).
- **Companies ceasing to be a Smaller Reporting Company, Foreign Private Issuer, or Controlled Company**: 6-month phase-in (for former FPIs and former SRCs as applicable) or IPO-style phase-in (for former Controlled Companies) to reach full compliance (https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf; https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/08/30/2024-19496/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-order-granting-approval-of-a-proposed-rule).

**Cure period:** If a company loses majority-independent-board compliance due to one vacancy or one director's independence ending for reasons beyond their reasonable control, it has until the earlier of its next annual shareholders meeting or one year from the event (or 180 days if the annual meeting falls within 180 days of the event) to regain compliance, with immediate notice to Nasdaq (Rule 5605(b)(1)(A)).

## 5. Summary Table

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| General definition | Not an Executive Officer/employee; no relationship that, in the board's opinion, interferes with independent judgment (Rule 5605(a)(2)) |
| Employment look-back | 3 years (director or Family Member as Executive Officer) |
| Compensation cap | $120,000 in any 12 consecutive months within prior 3 years (excl. board/committee fees, non-executive Family Member pay, qualified retirement/non-discretionary comp) |
| Business payments cap | Greater of 5% of recipient's consolidated gross revenues or $200,000 (current + past 3 fiscal years) |
| Auditor ties | Current partner, or partner/employee who worked on the audit within past 3 years |
| Board composition | Majority independent (Rule 5605(b)(1)) |
| Committees | Audit: ≥3 independent; Compensation: ≥2 independent; Nominations: fully independent (or majority-independent board acts) |
| Key exemptions | Controlled Companies (>50% voting power); Foreign Private Issuers (home-country practice); debt/preferred-only and passive issuers; IPO/transition phase-ins of up to 12 months |

**Uncertainty notes:** (1) The exceptions to paragraph (D) (investment-income and charitable-matching carve-outs) were verified against secondary reproductions of the rule text (a company's board rules document and Nasdaq's published rule page excerpts) rather than a fully fetched primary rule text, since the Nasdaq Listing Center page could not be fetched directly; the core (A)–(G) text is corroborated by multiple SEC-filed rule filings. (2) The interim-employment carve-out under (A)/(B) derives from Nasdaq staff interpretive practice as summarized in proxy statements, not from the rule text itself. (3) Rule citations reflect the rule as amended through the August 2024 phase-in amendments (SR-NASDAQ-2024-019); dollar thresholds ($120,000/$200,000) have been unchanged since at least 2012 per the SEC filings cited above.
