# Trust-Building Mechanisms in Argentina, Colombia, and Brazil
## UX Research Report: Gig Platform Expansion into High-Informality Latin American Markets

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Trust-building in Argentina, Colombia, and Brazil cannot be imported from US/European gig playbooks, because the operating environment is defined by mass informality: **55.9% of Colombian employment was informal in 2024** (DANE), **~42–50% in Argentina** (OECD/national sources), and **38.9% in Brazil** (IBGE, Q3 2024). In these markets, platforms are not adding a trust layer on top of functioning formal institutions — they are often the *first* trust infrastructure many users have encountered that is not family, word-of-mouth, or cash-in-hand.

Four findings matter most for UX design:

1. **Ratings work differently on the two sides of the marketplace.** Consumer-side reputation (e.g., Mercado Libre's color-coded thermometer) is the region's most mature trust asset, but worker-side ratings are experienced as surveillance and deactivation risk, driving circumvention behaviors like account rental (up to ~30% of gig accounts in Mexico, a regional proxy, per Rest of World).
2. **Identity verification rails are nationally specific and state-anchored.** Brazil verifies against CPF/SERPRO and CNH QR codes; Argentina against RENAPER's Sistema de Identidad Digital; Colombia against the cédula and Registraduría. A single global KYC vendor flow will underperform local registry-backed checks.
3. **Payment escrow expectations are shaped by Pix (Brazil) and Mercado Pago (region-wide)** — instant, free, and (in Brazil's case) irrevocable. Escrow must be paired with a visible, fast refund promise (Mercado Libre's "Compra Garantida" sets the benchmark: 21–30 day coverage, immediate refunds to wallet).
4. **Prior experience with trust systems is the strongest adoption lever.** Generalized interpersonal trust is very low (Latinobarómetro 2023: Brazil 4%, Colombia 17%, Argentina 28%, vs. 16% regional average), yet Brazil shows the region's highest digital-payment adoption — because users transfer trust from *institutional and familiar* systems (a central-bank-run Pix, a dominant marketplace, WhatsApp word-of-mouth) rather than from strangers. Familiarity with a platform's business model directly and indirectly drives intention to use (Brazilian survey, n=898).

---

## 2. Market Context: Informality Baseline

| Country | Informal employment share | Source & vintage |
|---|---|---|
| Colombia | **55.9%** national (2024 full year; down 0.5 pp from 56.4% in 2023); **42.5%** in 13 metro areas; **83.2–84.1%** in rural dispersed areas | DANE GEIH bulletins (https://www.dane.gov.co/files/operaciones/GEIH/bol-GEIHEISS-oct-dic2024.pdf) |
| Argentina | **~50%** (2023, internationally comparable ILO definition); **~42%** of total employment (end-2024, national household survey covering 31 largest urban areas) | OECD Economic Survey Argentina 2025 (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-argentina-2025_27dd6e27-en/full-report/devising-a-comprehensive-strategy-to-foster-formalisation_a2bd1fe7.html) |
| Brazil | **38.9%** of occupied population (quarter ending Oct 2024) = record **40.28 million** informal workers; **26.6%** of private-sector employees (14.2M of 53.4M) lacked a signed work card (carteira) in Q4 2024 — a year-end series record | IBGE Pnad Contínua (https://agenciadenoticias.ibge.gov.br/agencia-noticias/2012-agencia-de-noticias/noticias/41930-no-terceiro-trimestre-de-2024-desocupacao-recua-em-sete-unidades-da-federacao; https://www.poder360.com.br/poder-economia/266-dos-trabalhadores-eram-informais-no-4o-tri-de-2024/) |

**Quantitative observations:**
- The Colombia–Brazil informality gap is **17.0 percentage points** (55.9 − 38.9), meaning Colombian users arrive with far less exposure to formal contracts, payroll, or consumer-protection regimes.
- Within Colombia, the metro–rural informality gap is **~40.7 pp** (83.2 − 42.5) — rural/peri-urban users will have near-zero prior experience with formal dispute or verification systems.
- Within Brazil, state-level informality ranges from **26.8% (Santa Catarina) to 56.9% (Pará)** — a **30.1 pp spread** (IBGE). São Paulo (30.6%) behaves like a formal market; Pará or Maranhão (55.6%) do not. Sub-national segmentation is not optional.
- Region-wide, ILO harmonized data put Latin America & the Caribbean at **51.7% informal employment** (https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2025-01/Americas_Informality%20Regional%20statistical%20profile.pdf); the ILO/ECLAC monitor shows informality essentially flat pre- vs. post-pandemic (50.7% in 2022 vs. 50.6% in 2019), with Argentina *rising* 4.1 pp in 2022 (https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/%40americas/%40ro-lima/%40sro-santiago/documents/publication/wcms_887641.pdf).

**UX implication:** a large share of your supply side has never had a formal employment relationship, a credit score, or a formal receipt (factura). Trust mechanisms must teach, not just verify.

---

## 3. Rating Systems

### 3.1 Consumer-side reputation: Mercado Libre as the regional reference
Mercado Libre — with **78.6% of Argentine marketplace traffic** in 2022 (ECLAC, https://www.cepal.org/sites/default/files/project/files/annual-report_argentina.pdf) — operates the region's most legible reputation system:

- **Color-thermometer levels** (gray → red → orange → yellow → light green → green), computed from fulfilled orders over the trailing 3 months plus the current month (or the full record if fewer than 40 fulfilled orders); the first evaluation occurs after **10 orders** (https://global-selling.mercadolibre.com/learning-center/news/seller-reputation-learn-how-it-works).
- **Green requires a complaint rate ≤ 2%** and dispatch within **48 working hours** (same source).
- **Reputation is computed per country** — a seller must maintain it separately in each marketplace (same source), which matters for your multi-country launch.
- Critically for informal sellers, Mercado Libre runs **Reputation Recovery / Startup programs**: sellers with no rating or red/orange/yellow status can post a **financial guarantee** and receive a *fixed green level* for a set period (documented example: max 5 issues allowed, 365-day protection), with the deposit partially or fully returned based on claims, cancellations, and delays — live in Argentina (MLA), Brazil (MLB), Chile (MLC), and Colombia (MCO) (https://developers.mercadolibre.com.ar/en_us/manage-packages/reputation-recovery). This is effectively **escrow-backed reputation bootstrapping** — a mechanism that lets an informal seller with zero history transact credibly on day one.

### 3.2 Rating integrity is a trust bottleneck in Colombia
A PLS-SEM study of Mercado Libre Colombia buyers (**n = 326**) found that **perceived fake reviews negatively affect trust in the rating system**, that high-quality reviews positively influence all forms of trust, and that **trust in the rating system mediates** the relationship between fake-review perception and overall customer experience (Frontiers in Communication, https://public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1460321/pdf). In a market where 55.9% of workers are informal and reviews substitute for credentials, one visible fake-review scandal damages the entire trust stack.

### 3.3 Worker-side ratings: control, not reassurance
- Rio de Janeiro delivery-worker research documents that platforms "monitor and rate workers' performance based on metrics such as punctuality and customer reviews, and these ratings can lead to **'deactivations'**" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0lsdk5n1c3q).
- Chilean domestic-worker platform research identifies **"Use of Ratings and Reputation"** as a theme experienced as surveillance that weakens, rather than supports, the employment relationship (https://exa.ai/library/publication/pg1z8fwxy28).
- Brazilian research on four major platforms (iFood, Rappi, Uber, 99 — jointly ~4 million workers) characterizes platform-worker communication via ratings, classifications, and algorithmic management as marked by "disequilibriums of information, power and vigilance" (https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/10701230.pdf).
- **Circumvention is quantified:** banned workers rent accounts from colleagues; one union estimate cited by Rest of World puts **as many as 30% of ~500,000 gig accounts in Mexico** (~150,000 accounts) in someone else's hands, with the same dynamic documented in Brazil (https://restofworld.org/2024/gig-work-account-rental/). Any rating system you build will be gamed via account sharing unless verification is continuous (see §4).

### 3.4 Rating portability
An experiment with **180 actual clients of five gig platforms** found imported (cross-platform) ratings build trust **only when the job type matches and the worker has no within-platform ratings** — otherwise clients discount them (Electronic Markets, https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/elmark/v33y2023i1d10.1007_s12525-023-00655-2.html). Since workers "typically cannot take their ratings from one platform to another," reputation lock-in is real: new workers on your platform start from zero, and recruiting established workers away from incumbents means their reputation capital does not transfer.

**Design implications:** (a) adopt a coarse, color/level-based consumer reputation with a guaranteed-coverage bootstrapping program for zero-history informal sellers; (b) invest in review-quality controls (verified-transaction badges, anomaly detection) especially for Colombia; (c) for workers, pair ratings with transparent thresholds, warnings before deactivation, and an appeal path (see §6) — both because courts increasingly require it and because perceived arbitrariness drives account rental; (d) do not expect imported ratings to substitute for early within-platform history.

## 4. Identity Verification

### 4.1 Brazil: registry-backed, biometric, fast
- **SERPRO Datavalid** validates identity "directly on government databases": facial validation with liveness, CNH (driver's license) QR-code decoding, and CPF status checks, in real time via REST API (https://apicenter.estaleiro.serpro.gov.br/documentacao/datavalid/en/).
- Scale: SERPRO holds records for **220+ million** citizens/residents and **~83.7 million validated driving licenses** (https://docs.bynn.com/docs/government-registry-verification-brazil); **65+ million digital CNHs** are in circulation, with QR codes issued since May 2017 and selfie-to-Senatran face matching available (https://www.hopae.com/blog/hopae-launches-digital-cnh-verification; https://docs.didit.me/api-reference/database-validation/brazil/cnh-facial-qrcode).
- Commercial KYC rails advertise **R$0.12 per check, <3-second verification, false-positive rejection below 0.1%**, with LGPD audit trails (https://biblue.com.br/casos-de-uso/onboarding-digital).
- KYC is legally mandatory (Law 9,613/1998; Central Bank Circular 3,978/2020's risk-based regime with 10-year retention), so Brazilian users are *accustomed* to biometric onboarding from banking (https://www.guep.com.br/en/solucoes/kyc/).

### 4.2 Argentina: state-run RENAPER verification
- The **Sistema de Identidad Digital (SID)**, built by the state, allows entities to "validate identity remotely and in real time with RENAPER via biometric authentication factors (facial recognition) and DNI photo" (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/interior/renaper/sid-sistema-de-identidad-digital).
- "Paquete 1 – Biometría más datos": user photographs DNI front/back, takes a liveness selfie; the system extracts data, checks DNI validity, matches against RENAPER records, and returns a **match score plus public data** (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/sid/modalidades-y-productos/paquete1; https://www.argentina.gob.ar/sid/proceso-de-verificacion).
- Access requires compliance with **Ley 25.326** (data protection) and consent-based data cession (Art. 11) (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/sid/modalidades-y-productos). Fingerprint (SOAP) and face-photo (REST) validation services exist, though liveness detection is out of scope for some (same source).

### 4.3 Colombia: cédula-centric, multi-vendor, fraud-heavy
- Verification flows center on the **cédula de ciudadanía** (legacy yellow card and new digital format), cédula de extranjería, and the Venezuelan **Permiso por Protección Temporal (PPT)** — essential given Venezuelan migrant couriers are a documented worker segment in Bogotá (https://perfilesycapacidades.javeriana.edu.co/es/publications/infrastructuring-platform-delivery-work-exclusions-coercions-and-/).
- Vendor economics: full KYC ~**$0.33/session**; a fast provider-backed cédula lookup ~**$0.20**; direct Registraduría checks have **~75% coverage** (https://didit.me/solutions/countries/colombia/). Local vendors (Verifik, SofId, Identica) bundle OCR, selfie-vs-document, liveness, OTP, and SARLAFT/SAGRILAFT watchlist screening (https://verifik.co/en/identity-verification-colombia/; https://sofid.co/; https://identica.co/).
- Documented fraud pressures: **synthetic cédulas** riding fintech/wallet onboarding waves, forgery across legacy/digital formats, and remittance-corridor mule networks (https://didit.me/solutions/countries/colombia/). One Colombian forensic firm states identity-substitution losses can exceed **COP 2,500 million per year** (https://www.asisa.com.co/index.html). Data handling falls under **Ley 1581** (https://veryficol.com/).

### 4.4 Cross-cutting findings
- **Verification is becoming a regulatory expectation for platforms**: Paraguay's pending platform-law framework would make "identity verification mechanisms for all individuals in the platform ecosystem" mandatory — a signal of regional regulatory direction (Fairwork Brazil 2025, https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2025/09/Fairwork-Brazil-Report-2025-ENG_FINAL.pdf).
- **One-time onboarding verification is insufficient**: the account-rental phenomenon (§3.3) means the verified person and the person performing the gig diverge over time. Periodic re-verification (e.g., selfie checkpoints at login or delivery handoff, as Brazilian logistics vendors offer) is the emerging norm (https://driverid.com.br/en/driver-id-platform/).
- **Inclusion trade-off:** strict registry matching can exclude migrants and rural users (Colombia's Registraduría direct check covers only ~75%). Offer tiered verification — registry-backed where possible, document + liveness fallback elsewhere — or you will replicate the exclusion patterns documented among Venezuelan workers.

## 5. Payment Escrow Approaches

### 5.1 Brazil: Pix redefined the baseline
- Pix (central-bank-run, launched Nov 2020) is used by **over 170 million consumers — 93% of Brazil's adult population** — while **60 million Brazilians lack a credit card**; Pix volume reached **USD 6.7 trillion in 2025 (+34% YoY)**, approaching **7.9 billion monthly transactions** in December (EBANX, https://business.ebanx.com/en/press-room/press-releases/pix-to-approach-8-billion-monthly-transactions-as-it-marks-five-year-milestone-ebanx-study-finds). Arithmetic: 170M ÷ 0.93 ≈ **182.8M adults**, so Pix reaches essentially the entire adult market, including most of the 60M shut out of card rails. Pix surpassed combined credit+debit card *transaction counts* in 2023 and is projected to reach **50% of e-commerce by 2028** (Reuters/Ebanx, https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/instant-payment-system-pix-poised-capture-half-brazils-e-commerce-market-by-2028-2026-02-10/).
- Among small (largely informal) businesses, **97% use Pix** and it accounts for **~90% of non-cash business revenues** — though most flows through *personal* accounts (IPA/J-PAL, Espírito Santo survey n=1,151, https://poverty-action.org/how-pix-powering-open-finance-brazil). A consumer survey puts Pix as the main payment method for **80% of consumers (55% online)** and describes the national mood as **"agilidade com medo"** — agility with fear (CNDL/SPC Brasil, https://site.cndl.org.br/pix-e-o-meio-de-pagamento-mais-utilizado-por-80-dos-consumidores-aponta-cndlspc-brasil/).
- **The escrow problem:** Pix settles instantly and *irrevocably* — 63.4 billion transactions in 2024 (https://jamesroca.com/insights/latam_p1/) — so the central bank built the **Mecanismo Especial de Devolução (MED)**, a special-return mechanism for contested transactions tracked in official fraud statistics (https://dadosabertos.bcb.gov.br/gl/dataset/pix). Average Pix scam losses rose **21% to R$2,540** in H1 2025 (implying ~R$2,100 in H1 2024: 2,540 ÷ 1.21 ≈ 2,099), with 65% of cases now routed to corporate accounts (up from 42%) (Silverguard/Valor, https://valorinternational.globo.com/markets/news/2025/10/27/average-loss-from-pix-scams-rises-21percent.ghtml). Marketplace scams are explicitly named as a driver.

**Design implication:** in Brazil, users will *expect* Pix, but platform-mediated escrow (funds held until service completion) plus a visible fraud-refund promise is what differentiates you from raw P2P Pix, which users already associate with scam risk.

### 5.2 Region-wide: Mercado Pago's "Compra Garantida" as the escrow benchmark
- Coverage: money back if the product doesn't arrive (**21–28 days from purchase** depending on page) or on regret/defect (**up to 30 days from receipt**); refunds are **immediate to the Mercado Pago wallet** when paid with balance or boleto; QR and off-platform payments are excluded (https://www.mercadolivre.com.br/compra-garantida; https://www.mercadolivre.com.br/l/conheca-seus-beneficios).
- It activates **automatically** with any Mercado Pago checkout — no opt-in — and a parallel **Seller Protection Program** shields compliant sellers (with shipping proof) from chargebacks (https://www.mercadopago.com.br/blog/o-que-sao-compras-garantidas; https://www.mercadopago.com.br/blog/como-oferecer-compra-garantida).
- In Argentina specifically, Mercado Pago dominates P2P and business payments alongside CVU/alias instant transfers and QR (https://answerforme.io/en/blog/whatsapp-business-argentina-guide-2026).

### 5.3 Colombia: superapp wallets and cash-in networks
- **RappiPay Davivienda** (JV granted a banking license June 2022) offers wallet, transfers, and card products "without requiring any paperwork," with cash-in via agents, bank transfers, and Davivienda ATMs (https://inclusivemoney.com/fintech/rappi-pay; https://ir.davivienda.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/press-release-rappipay-davivienda.pdf). Within two years of launch it served **730,000+ customers with 20M+ transactions/year** (https://ir.davivienda.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/DAV_Rappi_Davivienda_-Press_Release_03092021.pdf) — evidence that low-paperwork, agent-assisted cash-in is the adoption unlock in a cash-heavy market.
- Research on **Movii** (Colombia's first fintech under a non-banking e-money license) shows wallet networks grow in transactional complexity as users discover P2B and B2B uses, with COVID accelerating adoption (https://ideas.repec.org/p/bdr/borrec/1157.html; https://www.suomenpankki.fi/globalassets/bof/en/research/seminars-and-conferences/conferences-and-workshops/documents/eopx2021/leon_the-adoption-of-a-mobile-payment-system-the-user-perspective.pdf).
- **WhatsApp-based escrow is an emerging pattern**: startups like Kustodia offer in-chat stablecoin payments and "escrow onchain" (funds held in a neutral environment until agreed conditions are verified), motivated by the claim that **the region loses ~20% of e-commerce revenue to fraud annually** and WhatsApp reaches ~80% of the population / 530M daily users region-wide (https://www.elobservador.com/argentina/economia/los-pagos-cripto-llegan-whatsapp-asi-funciona-la-startup-que-protege-transacciones-america-latina-n6045950).

final.content:
# Platform Selection Research Report: Farm Management & Traceability for a 5,000-Member Multi-Origin Coffee Cooperative

**Prepared for:** Cooperative leadership (Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia)
**Scope:** AtSource (Olam/ofi), Fairtrace (FLOCERT), and alternative platforms, assessed against six criteria: basic-phone usability, GPS mapping in mountainous terrain, certification integration (Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade), multi-language support, offline functionality, and cost per farmer.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

The two platforms named in the task brief are frequently misunderstood, and the misunderstanding changes the entire procurement strategy:

- **AtSource is not a platform a cooperative can buy.** It is ofi's (Olam Food Ingredients) proprietary sustainable-sourcing solution for *ofi's customers* — the brands and manufacturers who buy Olam's coffee, cocoa, and other crops. Its farmer-facing data-collection engine, the **Olam Farmer Information System (OFIS)**, is deployed by ofi's own field teams inside ofi's supply chains. A cooperative accesses it only by selling through ofi/Olam, in which case onboarding is effectively bundled into the commercial relationship at ofi's cost (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html; https://www.ofi.com/en-us/sustainability/ofi-farmer-information-system).
- **Fairtrace is not a farm management or GPS tool.** It is FLOCERT's mandatory transaction-reporting and assurance platform for Fairtrade-certified companies — it records volumes, Minimum Price, and Premium via "virtual handshakes" between trading partners. It is web-based, requires Fairtrade certification for access, and is included in certification fees rather than sold separately (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf; https://www.flocert.net/glossary/fairtrace/).

The practical architecture that emerges from the evidence is a **two-layer stack**: (1) free/mandatory certification-system tools (Fairtrade's Plot Insights + Fairtrace; Rainforest Alliance's RACP + MultiTrace), plus (2) a commercially procured or open-source **first-mile farm management layer** (Farmforce, Koltiva, SourceTrace, Fairfood Trace, or KoboToolbox/TerraTrac) that collects farmer data, maps plots offline, and feeds the certification systems.

**Headline cost finding:** For 5,000 farmers, documented field-mapping costs range from **~$0.30 per farmer** (TechnoServe Kenya, open-source app) to **~$4 per farm** (Ethiopia EUDR pilot) to **$11–32 per farmer** (commercial mapping services), while enterprise compliance software runs **€10,000–50,000/year plus €5,000–90,000 setup**. A realistic mid-case budget for the cooperative is roughly **$25,000–41,000 in year one (~$5–8 per farmer)** for a commercial first-mile platform, or as little as **~$1,500 (~$0.30/farmer)** for a staff-run open-source approach — excluding certification fees themselves.

---

## 2. What Each Named Platform Actually Is

### 2.1 AtSource (Olam / ofi) — a buyer-side sourcing solution, not a cooperative tool

AtSource is described by ofi as "a sustainable sourcing solution that provides traceability to a product's origin and transparency on key supply chain sustainability challenges through data and insights," sold in tiers (Entry, AtSource+, AtSource∞) with over 350 metrics, third-party assurance, and carbon/water footprint calculators (https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html; https://www.atsource.io/news/how-a-one-stop-data-shop-is-spicing-up-sustainability.html).

Critically, its governance page states: **"AtSource is open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains"** — i.e., only supply chains that ofi/Olam itself buys from (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html). There is no pricing, no self-service onboarding, and no cooperative subscription. The cooperative's only route to AtSource is a sourcing relationship with ofi.

The farmer-facing machinery behind AtSource is **OFIS**, and it is genuinely relevant to this cooperative's requirements — but only via that relationship:

- **Scale and purpose:** OFIS is a survey tool ofi built because "many of these farmers live and work in isolation with no access to the internet." Over **550,000 farmers in more than 30 countries** are registered, and OFIS data feeds AtSource (https://www.ofi.com/en-us/sustainability/ofi-farmer-information-system).
- **GPS mapping:** OFIS was developed in 2014 "with a GPS mapping system, so that smallholder supply chains could be geo-spatially identified"; field staff "record GPS data points directly on the ground for farms and social infrastructure," and each bag of produce is geo-tagged for farm-to-fork traceability (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-shares-tech-with-wildlife-conservation.html; https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/07/New-OFIS-Brochure-1.pdf).
- **Offline capability:** The OFIS Enumerator app "supports data collection where internet access is limited/non-existent" (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.olam.digital.ofis&hl=en_US), and an FAO case study confirms that "due to limitations in network coverage and the cost of data services, information is usually collected offline and synced when connectivity is restored" (https://dvi-ke.fao.org/digital_solutions_details.php?id=120).
- **Basic-phone usability:** Farmers themselves need no smartphone — OFIS generates personalized farm development plans whose advice "can be texted straight to the farmer's mobile phone," plus mobile payment wallets (https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/06/OFIS-Press-Release-05.06.2017.pdf).
- **Languages:** OFIS was implemented across "8 products, 21 countries and 9 languages" (2017 figure) (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/one-stop-tech-platform-yield-traceability-financial-access.html).
- **Coffee and mountain-terrain relevance:** OFIS was granted to the Wildlife Conservation Society for **20,000+ smallholder coffee farmers in southern Sumatra** to map farm boundaries and monitor coffee entering supply chains around Bukit Barisan Selatan National Park — directly analogous to the cooperative's Indonesian terrain (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-shares-tech-with-wildlife-conservation.html).

**Verdict:** Exclude AtSource from the RFP. Treat it as a potential *byproduct* of selling through ofi: if ofi sources from the cooperative, OFIS registration and AtSource visibility come with the relationship at no cost to the cooperative.

### 2.2 Fairtrace (FLOCERT) — mandatory Fairtrade transaction reporting, not farm management

Fairtrace is "FLOCERT's online collaboration and assurance platform for all certified companies," capturing "Fairtrade transaction data (volumes, Minimum Price and Premium)" via virtual handshakes (https://www.flocert.net/glossary/fairtrace/). The Fairtrade Assurance Rules make it compulsory: certified organisations "are furthermore required to use the transaction reporting platform Fairtrace" (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/assurance/Fairtrade-Assurance-Rules-Guidelines.pdf). Around **6,000 organisations** use it, reporting **more than 500,000 transactions per year** (https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/).

Key operational facts:

- **Who uses it:** Cooperative *staff* (registered Reporting Contacts), not farmers. Producers generally do not report sales in Fairtrace; they verify transactions reported by their customers, and report only direct purchases from certified producers if they hold trader certification (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/07/SAM-FairtraceUserGuide-TR-19-en.pdf).
- **Access:** "Only FLOCERT certified customers get access to Fairtrace" (https://fairtrace-account.flocert.net/assets/SAM_FairtraceLoginManual_TR_18_en.pdf).
- **Cost:** Fairtrace is not separately priced. FLOCERT's Terms state Certification Fees cover "access to and running the relevant Tools" (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2026/09/Certification-Terms-and-Conditions.pdf, §5.1.1), under an "all-in" fee model with no extra charges for audits or travel (https://www.flocert.net/fairtrade-fee-calculator/). Certification cost itself is quote-based via FLOCERT's fee calculator; no public per-farmer figure exists in the evidence gathered.
- **Offline:** None claimed — it is a web platform with quarterly reporting deadlines (report within 30 days of quarter close; verify partner transactions within 30 days) (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf).
- **Languages:** FLOCERT publishes support material in English and Portuguese (https://www.flocert.net/technical-support/; https://www.flocert.net/pt/apoio-tecnico/); full interface language coverage was not confirmed in the evidence gathered.

**The companion tool that matters for GPS:** Fairtrade's **Plot Insights** — "Fairtrade's digital tool for securely validating, managing and sharing geolocation data," with plot-level deforestation risk analysis from Satelligence, **"Free for all certified cocoa and coffee SPOs,"** available in **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, and Vietnamese** (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf). It accepts points and polygons (polygons mandatory for plots ≥4 ha), converts data to the EUDR TRACES GeoJSON format, lets cooperatives assign plots to sales contracts, and is connected to Fairtrace via the **GeoLink API** so exporters can pull geolocation data into contracts (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf). Fairtrade explicitly frames this as relieving a cost burden: "Farmers are having to adopt new digital tools and map farm plots, which is an expensive burden… With Plot Insights, Fairtrade coffee and cocoa cooperatives have a free platform" (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html).

**Verdict:** If the cooperative is or becomes Fairtrade-certified, Fairtrace is non-negotiable but costless as a line item (bundled into certification fees), and Plot Insights gives it a free geolocation/EUDR backbone in three of its needed languages (Spanish, Indonesian, English — but not Amharic).

---

## 3. The Certification-System Context Both Certifications Impose

Any platform the cooperative selects must produce data in the exact formats these systems demand:

**Rainforest Alliance (RA):** Certificate Holders "must submit geolocation data to the Rainforest Alliance platform" — points and polygons for all farm units, WGS84 (EPSG:4326), decimal degrees, **at least 4 decimals** (base requirement) or **6 decimals** under EUDR-aligned criteria, with **polygons required for farm units ≥4 ha** (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex-v12; https://rainforest-alliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/EUDR-Webinar-January-2024.pdf). All coffee/cocoa certificate holders are now audited against EUDR-aligned requirements (integrated assessments binding from June 16, 2025 policies; ~50% of coffee/cocoa Certificate Holders had already opted in by early 2025) (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/eudr-and-the-rainforest-alliance-certification-program-upgrading-our-approach). Certified volumes must also be traced on RA's **MultiTrace** platform (quarterly transaction reporting; being migrated to a new traceability platform inside MyRA/RACP) (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/traceability-for-fresh-processed-fruits-vegetables-and-cut-flowers; https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/new-traceability-platform-everything-you-need-to-know). Like Fairtrade, RA provides these systems to certificate holders as part of certification — no separate platform purchase.

**Fairtrade:** Coffee Standard requirement 3.1.6 and Cocoa 3.4.5 require geolocation for 100% of member plots, annual registry updates, polygons for plots ≥4 ha, and define high-risk plots as within 500 m of deforestation or 200 m of protected areas (Plot Insights guidance PDF, above). Fairtrade's Satelligence forest layer has a stated accuracy of **81–93% across South America, Africa, and Asia** at 10 m resolution using Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf) — the only quantified accuracy figure found for any satellite monitoring layer in this research.

**Implication:** The winning first-mile platform must export WGS84 decimal-degree points/polygons and GeoJSON, support polygon capture for ≥4 ha plots, and link plots to transactions. This is now a table-stakes filter, not a differentiator.

---

## 4. Candidate Solutions for the Farm-Management Layer

### 4.1 Farmforce — strongest documented coffee/EUDR track record among vendors

- **Functionality:** Digital farmer database with unique farmer/field IDs, photos, bio-data; field staff map **GPS polygons of individual fields** via mobile app or shapefile import; Global Forest Watch integration for deforestation checks; loan/input tracking; explicit support for "Certifications & auditing (Organic, Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance)" and child-labour monitoring (https://farmforce.com/solutions/farmers-database-gps-mapping/; https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/; https://farmforce.com/).
- **Offline:** "Our solutions are built to run offline," with design principles of "gamification and low literacy levels" (https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/).
- **Cooperative fit:** A dedicated cooperatives/aggregators/SMEs solution line (https://farmforce.com/solutions/cooperatives/).
- **Documented coffee result:** The Farm Africa/ECOM pilot in Ethiopia's forested highlands (Bale and Illubabor, Aug 2025 onward, 8 months, Royal Norwegian Embassy-funded) onboarded **4,500+ smallholder producers, mapped ~4,550 ha of wild forest coffee, collected 3,500+ signed EUDR consent surveys**, and produced an ECTA-compliant dataset — a near-exact analogue for the cooperative's Ethiopian operation (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/).
- **Cost (low confidence):** Software directories list a flat **NOK 330/year** starting price with implementation estimated at **NOK 55,000–220,000** (https://softwarefinder.com/facility-management-software/farmforce; https://www.getapp.ie/software/2071368/farmforce; https://www.capterra.ie/software/189458/farmforce). At ~10.6 NOK/USD, that is roughly **USD 31/year** subscription plus **USD 5,200–20,800** implementation. These are third-party directory figures, possibly outdated and likely for a base tier; real cooperative pricing for 5,000 farmers across three countries must come from a direct quote. Treat as indicative only.

### 4.2 Koltiva (KoltiTrace) — strongest presence in the cooperative's three origins

- Swiss-Indonesian company servicing **440,000–475,000 farmers across 17 countries**, operating in **Indonesia, Colombia, Ethiopia**, Mexico, Uganda, Brazil and others — the only vendor found with documented field operations in all three of the cooperative's countries (https://www.koltiva.com/koltitrace; https://www.koltiva.com/post/koltiva-empowers-475-000-coffee-producers-worldwide-and-strengthens-indonesia-s-leadership-in-sustai).
- KoltiTrace combines "geolocation, supply chain mapping, and compliance reporting into one seamless system," with EUDR deforestation-risk mapping, legality checks, Cool Farm Tool integration, and — distinctively — **"boots on the ground" field verification and coaching services** (KoltiSkills), which matters where cooperative staff capacity is thin (https://www.koltiva.com/koltitrace; https://www.koltiva.com/post/koltiva-empowers-475-000-coffee-producers-worldwide-and-strengthens-indonesia-s-leadership-in-sustai).
- **Indonesian mountain-coffee proof point:** Adena Coffee (Indonesia) used Koltiva for EUDR-aligned data "directly from over 30 villages," supporting **1,900+ smallholders and 240 tonnes of coffee annually**, with emphasis on "farm-level geolocation accuracy, and continuous field verification" (https://www.koltiva.com/post/deforestation-free-coffee-supply-chains-adena-coffee-koltiva-eudr-compliance-transparency).
- Mobile apps are on Google Play (KoltiTrace MIS family); offline capability is implied by "digitizing producers and plot-level data collection, even in remote areas" but was not explicitly confirmed as offline-first in the evidence gathered.
- **Cost:** Not published; quote-based.

### 4.3 SourceTrace (DATAGREEN) — the only platform with documented feature-phone support

- Designed "for emerging markets with narrowband communications"; **DATAGREEN Remote transmits data using "Java-phones, Tablets and Smartphones"** — i.e., basic feature phones, not just Android — and "allows transactions in… the most demanding environments with low bandwidth or even without a permanent connection" (https://sourcetrace.com/the-platform/).
- "Farm perimeter plotting and area calculation using phone built-in GPS"; deployed with agribusinesses, **co-operatives**, and farmer producer companies across 37 countries including coffee; inbuilt **EUDR-format report generation**; manual and satellite-based farm mapping (https://sourcetrace.com/agriculture-apps/; https://sourcetrace.com/eudr-compliant-software/; https://sourcetrace.com/farm-management/).
- **Cost:** Not published; quote-based.

### 4.4 Fairfood Trace — cooperative-friendly blockchain traceability with consumer storytelling

- Blockchain platform connecting chain partners 1-up-1-down to the farmer; "easily accessible, even for smallholder farmers in low tech environments"; farmers connected via **Farmer Cards and a mobile field app**; digitises transactions and payments; QR-code consumer storytelling proven in coffee (Trabocca) and with the **Capucas Cooperative in Honduras** producing "100% traceable coffee" (https://fairfood.org/solutions-for-a-fair-supply-chain/blockchain-tool-trace/; https://fairfood.org/solutions-for-a-fair-supply-chain/trace-3/; https://fairfood.org/resources/from-honduras-to-europe-achieving-traceability-for-honduran-coffee/).
- Integrates with existing ERPs and other systems (https://fairfood.org/solutions-for-a-fair-supply-chain/blockchain-tool-trace/).
- **Cost:** Not published; NGO model suggests flexibility, but no evidence confirmed free or subsidised access.
- **Gap:** Offline capability of the field app and GPS polygon support were not confirmed in the gathered evidence.

### 4.5 Enveritas — free verification, but not a farm-management platform

A nonprofit providing **free verification of sustainability practices to producers** (buyers pay a per-pound fee), using satellite machine-learning to find coffee plots plus local field teams; fielded in Uganda, Ethiopia, and Sumatra among its first origins, with 90,000+ farm verifications across 30+ countries in 2024 (https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/projects-activities/enveritas_en; https://techcrunch.com/2018/08/30/enveritas-technology-lets-small-growers-tap-into-the-market-for-sustainable-coffee/; https://solve.mit.edu/solutions/2884; https://www.guidestar.org/profile/81-1681880). It complements — but does not replace — a management platform: it verifies and monitors; it does not run the cooperative's farmer registry, purchases, or certification data.

### 4.6 Open-source baseline: KoboToolbox / TerraTrac

TechnoServe's Kenya program supported **19 cooperative societies (48 washing stations)** to collect GPS data with **TerraTrac**, a free open-source app, including training on accuracy, backstopping to flag erroneous coordinates, and cost-tracking. Cooperatives' own calculations found **"the cost of data collection with the open-source, free-to-use app is about $0.30 per farmer,"** covering data-collector wages, a local guide, transport, and mobile internet (https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/). A separate Kenyan advisory notes KoboToolbox is free, supports GPS polygons and GeoJSON export for the EU's TRACES platform (https://agrosocialservices.co.ke/certification-compliance/eudr-gps-geolocation-kenya-coffee-cooperatives-2026/). This is the floor of the cost range — but it buys data collection only, not a managed platform, and demands more of cooperative staff.

---

## 5. Criterion-by-Criterion Comparison

| Criterion | AtSource/OFIS | Fairtrace (+Plot Insights) | Farmforce | Koltiva | SourceTrace | Fairfood Trace | Open-source (Kobo/TerraTrac) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Basic-phone usability** | Farmers receive SMS advice & mobile wallets; data entry by ofi field staff on Android | Web tool for cooperative staff, not farmers; no farmer interface | Field-staff app; farmer app (Connect) in pilot; low-literacy design | Field-staff apps + field-agent services | **Feature-phone (Java) support documented** | Farmer Cards for low-tech environments | Field-staff smartphone app only |
| **GPS in mountainous terrain** | GPS points recorded on the ground; proven on Sumatra coffee farms near BBSNP | Plot Insights validates/submits data; Satelligence layer 81–93% accuracy, 10 m resolution | GPS polygons per field; GFW deforestation overlay; Ethiopia highland pilot (4,550 ha) | Plot geolocation + continuous field verification; Indonesia mountain-coffee cases | Phone-GPS perimeter plotting + satellite mapping | Not confirmed | Phone GPS with local-guide protocols; backstopping for erroneous coordinates |
| **RA / Fairtrade integration** | Feeds ofi's AtSource; supports buyer compliance claims | **Native**: Fairtrace is the Fairtrade system; Plot Insights outputs EUDR TRACES GeoJSON | Claims support for Organic, Fairtrade, RA audits | EUDR + RA/Fairtrade complementarity claimed; CFT integration | EUDR-format reports; certification modules | Supports sustainability claims/proof; label integration unclear | GeoJSON for TRACES; format-compliant with RA/Fairtrade submissions |
| **Multi-language** | OFIS: 9 languages (2017) | Plot Insights: EN, ES, PT, FR, **Bahasa Indonesia**, VN; Fairtrace: EN/PT confirmed | Not confirmed | Not confirmed (strong Indonesia presence implies Bahasa) | Not confirmed | Not confirmed | Kobo: Swahili UI noted (Kenya source); others unverified |
| **Offline** | **Confirmed**: offline collection, sync on reconnect | No (web-based) | **Confirmed**: "built to run offline" | Implied ("even in remote areas"), not explicit | **Confirmed**: low-bandwidth/no-connection design | Not confirmed | Offline forms standard |
| **Cost for 5,000-farmer coop** | Not purchasable; bundled with ofi sourcing | Fairtrace bundled in Fairtrade certification fee; Plot Insights **free** | ~USD 31/yr + USD 5,200–20,800 implementation (directory figures, low confidence) | Quote-based | Quote-based | Quote-based | ~$0.30/farmer collection cost; $0 software |

**Language gap to flag:** No platform in the evidence set explicitly confirms **Amharic** (or Ethiopian local languages such as Sidamo/Oromifa) support. Plot Insights covers Spanish (Colombia) and Bahasa Indonesia, but Ethiopia's language coverage is a live question to put to every vendor.

---

## 6. Cost Analysis for a 5,000-Farmer Cooperative

**Documented per-farmer benchmarks (all figures as reported by sources):**

1. **Open-source field collection (Kenya, TechnoServe/TerraTrac):** ~**$0.30/farmer** — includes enumerator wages, local guide, transport, internet (https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/).
2. **Documented cooperative mapping programme (Ethiopia):** ~**$4/farm** with trained local enumerators and phone-based capture (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr).
3. **Commercial mapping service, Indonesia:** Cooperative Registry (≤300 smallholders, GPS + polygons >4 ha, land docs) from IDR 55,000,000 ≈ **USD 3,400 → ~$11.3/farmer**; Regional (500+) from USD 7,500 → ~$15/farmer (https://eudrindonesia.com/eudr-smallholder-mapping-service-indonesia/).
4. **Kenyan service estimate:** KES 205,000–420,000 ≈ **USD 1,600–3,200 for a 100-member coop → $16–32/farmer**, stated as <1% of annual EU export revenue (https://agrosocialservices.co.ke/certification-compliance/eudr-gps-geolocation-kenya-coffee-cooperatives-2026/).
5. **Enterprise compliance software:** **€10,000–50,000/year plus €5,000–90,000 setup** (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr).

**Arithmetic for 5,000 farmers (year one):**

- **Lean / staff-run scenario:** 5,000 × $0.30 = **$1,500** total field cost; software $0. Per farmer: **$0.30**. Assumes cooperative field staff, training investment, and that staff absorb registry maintenance. Certification-system tools (Plot Insights, RACP/MultiTrace, Fairtrace) add $0 in platform fees.
- **Mid / commercial-platform scenario:** mapping at $4/farm: 5,000 × $4 = **$20,000**; plus Farmforce-style implementation NOK 55,000–220,000 ≈ **USD 5,200–20,800**; plus nominal subscription (~USD 31/yr per directory data). Year-one total ≈ **$25,200–40,800 → $5.04–8.16 per farmer**. Ongoing years fall to software subscription + periodic mapping updates (boundary changes are "occasional, not annual" per the Qelvyn analysis).
- **Full-service scenario:** vendor-executed mapping at $11–32/farmer: **$55,000–160,000 → $11–32 per farmer**, or enterprise software at €15,000–140,000 year-one (setup + annual) ≈ **USD 16,000–152,000 → $3.2–30 per farmer**. Appropriate only if the cooperative lacks field capacity and buyer/NGO co-funding is unavailable.

Also "Bennett & Checkel vs Pearl & Mahoney" — I should structure the report as:

1. Introduction: the two research programs and why the framing needs nuance.
2. Ontological and methodological foundations:
   - Bennett & Checkel: process tracing as within-case analysis of causal mechanisms; Bayesian updating (Bennett), interpretive pluralism (Checkel); mechanisms as intervening processes; Van Evera tests; Collier 2011; Beach & Pedersen.
   - Pearl: SCM, DAGs, do-calculus, ladder of causation; mechanisms as structural equations; counterfactuals via abduction-action-prediction; critique of "model-blind" inference.
   - Mahoney: Bayesian formalization of PT tests (2012); Two Cultures (with Goertz): set-theoretic, necessary/sufficient causation; equifinality friendly.
   - Key tension: Pearl's framework demands explicit causal graphs and treats mechanism identification as a graph-identification problem (front-door/back-door); PT treats mechanisms as empirical narratives with evidentiary tests; Mahoney bridges via Bayesian logic but stays set-theoretic; Checkel resists formalization.
3. Operationalizing causal mechanisms:
   - PT: entities/activities (Machamer et al. 2000; Beach & Pedersen), sequence, context; four tests; hoop/smoking gun etc.
   - Pearl: mechanism = invariant structural relation; do-operator severs it; mediation = direct/indirect effects; requires identification assumptions (sequential ignorability).
   - Mahoney: tests as likelihood ratios; mechanisms as "causal pathways" verified via necessary/sufficient evidence.
   - Tension: Pearl's critique that verbal mechanism talk without graphs is ambiguous; PT's critique that DAGs underrepresent temporal sequence, context, and agency; Russo-Williamson thesis as synthesis.
4. Equifinality:
   - PT: within-case tracing can discriminate among pathways; but equifinality complicates generalization; Bennett: PT is well-suited to identify which path in which case.
   - Pearl: DAGs can represent multiple paths; but Pearl's framework is about identifying effects given a graph, less about discovering which path in a case; counterfactual queries can handle multiple causes.
   - Mahoney/Goertz: set-theoretic causation embraces equifinality (multiple sufficient configurations); QCA formalizes it.
   - QCA: truth tables, minimization; logical remainders; critiques (Lucas & Szatrowski; Krogslund et al.; Hug; Thiem et al.); defenses (Ragin; Schneider & Wagemann; Fiss; robustness protocols Oana & Schneider).
5. Confounder identification:
   - Pearl: back-door criterion; front-door; do-calculus; IV; sensitivity (Cinelli & Hazlett 2020 as modern quantitative analog).
   - PT: alternative explanations as rival hypotheses; within-case evidence (sequence, mechanism) to rule out confounders; "causal process observations" (Humphreys & Friedman 2008? "The Theoretical... "? Humphreys & Friedman (2008) "The Theoretical Foundations of Counterfactual Thought Experiments in International Relations"? Not needed).
   - Mahoney: necessary/sufficient conditions reframing; "Two Cultures" claim that qualitative researchers handle confounders via within-case logic.
   - Tension: KKV selection-bias critique; Collier & Mahoney reply; Sekhon; post-treatment conditioning critique (Montgomery, Nyhan, Torres 2018) vs. mediation ambitions; Acharya et al. 2016 as bridge.
